Rationally Selected Utility -A New Theory of Riskless Choice

To fix (3)

To fix Ethics Approval Check

What we found

1 of 1 paper appeared to involve live data collection and lacked an ethics approval statement.

Show details

Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, but it was not present:

For subjects proceeding to Stage 2, participants were selected whose risk aversion during the BDM bidding procedure (which is known to be distinct from their risk aversion level during choice) was narrowly bounded (𝑝𝑜𝑤𝑒𝑟 𝑢𝑡𝑖𝑙𝑖𝑡𝑦 𝑐𝑢𝑟𝑣𝑎𝑡𝑢𝑟𝑒 𝑎𝑡 0.9 < 𝜌 < 1.1).

Unlike standard models in which a utility (or value) function and a noise term are fit by some form of a least squares procedure, to test our model we examine the error matrices produced by our subjects directly and compare them to the error matrices predicted by our theory.

If an experimentalist were to define 4 as the expected reference point when subjects were using this value function, they would observe a gain-loss asymmetry, a kind of loss aversion: If subjects were given a choice between $4 for sure or a 50/50 chance of either $3 or $5, they would prefer the $4 for sure.

Panel A: Empirical error matrices for the four subjects in the Uniform environment; color indicates the observed error rate, and numbers indicate the number of trials contributing to each cell.

Working Directory (setwd)

Best programming practice is to avoid setwd() in analysis code: it hardcodes an assumption about the working directory (often an absolute path on the author’s own machine), so the code breaks when run anywhere else. Keep the working directory as the caller sets it and use relative paths. No setwd() calls were found in any of the code files.

Package Installation (install.packages)

Best programming practice is to avoid install.packages() in analysis code: it installs software on whoever runs the script without asking, which is at minimum disruptive (an unexpected install, network access, a package version the author never tested against) and at worst a security risk if it points at an untrusted repository. Document required packages instead (a README, or a list of them: an renv.lock/DESCRIPTION for R, a requirements.txt for Python). No install.packages() calls were found in any of the code files.

Libraries / Imports

File paths

Every data path in the code works in the repository as deposited. 9 references matched several files sharing a name and could not be resolved by study group or folder; they were left unrewritten and flagged.

Execution

The Python code was run. Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 23 scripts: 0 ran without error, 0 errored, 10 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse, and 0 are written for Python 2 and not run. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions (e.g. in a requirements.txt). 13 scripts were not started, or stopped early, because the time for all scripts together had run out.

Self-reproducible output (JASP / jamovi / SPSS Viewer / Jupyter notebook)

1 JASP/jamovi/SPSS-Viewer/notebook file bundles the analyses and their saved results together, so the reported statistics are recoverable from the file itself, with nothing re-run. More detail

Power Analysis Check

No power analyses were detected.

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen’s d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.

We examined 572 columns across 156 data files.

Careless Responding

No file could be screened for careless responding.

What this does not cover. Only 0 of 156 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

How Ethics Approval Check works

This module searches for statements of ethics approval, IRB approval, institutional review board approval, and related terms.

Patterns are designed to capture:

Human research committee names - Institutional Review Board / IRB (US standard) - Independent Ethics Committee / IEC (ICH-GCP international clinical trial term) - Ethical/Ethics Review Board (generic) - Ethics (Advisory/Review) Committee/Board/Panel/Sub-committee - Research Ethics Committee/Board/Panel (UK/Canada/Australia) - Medical Ethics Committee - Human Subjects/Research Committee / Human Research Ethics (Advisory) Panel - Committee for/on the Protection of Human Subjects - Committee on (Health) Research Ethics - Office of Research Ethics - Abbreviations: IEC, REC, REB, ERB, METC, DEC. REC/REB/ERB/DEC are short enough to collide with unrelated jargon (e.g. REC as a recognition-heuristic model abbreviation, DEC as a decision-task label, Reb as an author surname), so these four require an ethics/approval/committee/board/panel/institutional/ protocol word within ~30 characters in the same sentence. IRB and IEC are kept unconstrained as they are not observed to collide in practice. - Dutch: Medisch-ethische toetsingscommissie (METC) - French: Comité d'éthique / Comité d'Ethique

Animal research committee names - Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee / IACUC (US standard) - Any sentence containing animal(s) and committee (or board/panel) within ~5 words of each other — catches Experimental Animal Care and Use Committee, Animal Ethics Committee, Animal Welfare Board, Animal Welfare Ethical Review Body, etc. - UK: Animal Welfare Ethical Review Body / AWERB - Dutch: Dierexperimentencommissie / DEC (see DEC constraint above); Instantie voor Dierenwelzijn / IvD - German: Tierversuchskommission / TvK (advisory committee under §15 Tierschutzgesetz) - French: Comité d'éthique en expérimentation animale / CEEA; Comité d'éthique animale - Spanish: Comité de ética en experimentación animal / CEEA

Approval phrasing - Ethics/Ethical (approval|clearance) [was] (granted|obtained|received|given|secured) - Ethically approved - Approved by the (ethics|irb|institutional|independent|local|review|research) ... - This/The study/protocol/experiment/procedures/methods/research [was] (approved|reviewed) by - Study was ethically approved - (Followed|met|follow) the ethical (guidelines|standards|requirements) - In accordance with ... ethical (guidelines|standards) - Ethics protocol - Approved under (protocol|reference|number)

Waiver / exemption - Ethics/Ethical (waiver|exemption) - IRB (waiver|exemption|exempt) - Exempted from (ethics|irb|institutional review) - Waived by the (ethics|irb|institutional|review) (committee|board) - Deemed exempt

Declaration of Helsinki - Declaration of Helsinki / Helsinki Declaration

Patterns are NOT designed to capture: - General ethical considerations or ethical dilemmas in study content - Mentions of “ethics” in theoretical or philosophical contexts - Author approval of a manuscript (e.g. “all authors approved the final version”) - Ethical behaviour as a measured variable (e.g. “ethical decision-making”) - URLs containing “ethics” in path components

Live data collection is detected by the internal helper .detect_live_data(), which searches for sentences indicating that data were collected directly from human or animal participants. Papers without any live-data signal are not flagged as missing ethics approval. The helper uses conservative patterns to avoid flagging secondary data analyses, computational experiments, or economics papers that analyse existing survey data. See .detect_live_data() for the full list of patterns and intentional exclusions.

A paper that states that no human or animal subjects took part (“no human subjects were involved”, “did not involve human participants”, or people taking part “not as subjects”) is not expected to have an ethics statement, whatever participant phrase it also has (see .detect_no_participants()). A negation near a participant phrase alone (“No participants were excluded”) does not count: it reports a study with participants.

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How Power Analysis Check works

This module uses regular expressions to identify sentences that contain a statistical power analysis. If specified by the user, it also uses a large language model (LLM) to extract information reported in power analyses, including the statistical test, sample size, alpha level, desired level of power, and magnitude and type of effect size.

The Power Analysis Check module uses regular expressions to identify sentences that contain a statistical power analysis. Without the use of an LLM, the module uses regular expressions to classify the power analysis as a-priori, sensitivity or post-hoc. With the use of an LLM, it checks if the power analysis is reported with all required information.

The regular expressions can miss power analyses, or fail to classify them correctly. The type of power analysis is often difficult to classify, which can easily be solved by explicitly specifying the type of power analysis as ‘a-priori’, ‘sensitivity’, or ‘post-hoc’. Note that ‘post-hoc’ or ‘observed’ power is rarely useful. The LLM can fail to identify information in the paper, and will not have access to information in paragraphs in the paper other than those that contain the word ‘power’. This package was validated by the Metacheck team on articles in Psychological Science.

This module was developed by Lisa DeBruine, Daniel Lakens and Cristian Mesquida

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 128 papers with 246 instances of power statements, 203 were correctly detected (true positives), 22 were missed (false negatives) and 21 were incorrectly detected (false positives). Overall, among all instances flagged as power statements, 90.6% were correct (positive predictive value).

How Preregistration Check works

Retrieve information from preregistrations in a standardised way, and make them easier to check.

The Preregistration Check module identifies preregistrations on the OSF and AsPredicted based on links in the manuscript, retrieves the preregistration text, and organizes the information into a template. The module retrieves text from the OSF with its API, and from AsPredicted with ResearchBox’s API when a ResearchBox key is set (see rbox_token()), or else from the preregistration’s web page. The information in the preregistration is returned. An AsPredicted link that could not be read is named in the report, with the reason.

The module can’t extract information from non-structured preregistration templates (i.e., where the preregistration is uploaded in a single text field) and it can’t retrieve information in preregistrations that are stored as text documents on the OSF.

If you want to extend the package to be able to download information from other preregistration sites, reach out to the Metacheck development team.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How Marginal Significance works

List all sentences that describe an effect as ‘marginally significant’.

The marginal module searches for regular expressions that match a predefined pattern. The list of terms is a subset of those listed in a blog post by Matthew Hankins. The module returns all sentences that match terms describing ‘marginally significant’ results.

Some of the terms identified might not be problematic in some contexts, and there are ways to describe ‘marginal significance’ that are not detected by the module.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 51 papers with 87 statements, this module correctly identified 38 statements (true positives) and incorrectly flagged 22 statements (false positives). It failed to detect 27 statements. Thus, among all statements flagged by the module, 63% were genuine cases (positive predictive value). However, the module missed 42% of all true statements (false negative rate).

How StatCheck works

Check consistency of p-values and test statistics

The Statcheck module runs Statcheck. Statcheck searches for regular expressions that match a predefined pattern, and identifies APA reported statistical tests. More information on the package can be found at https://github.com/cran/statcheck. The module only returns Statcheck results for t-tests and F-tests, as these are the only tests which have been validated, see https://osf.io/preprints/psyarxiv/tcxaj_v1/.

Statcheck was developed by Michèle Nuijten and Sascha Epskamp.

Statcheck considers p = 0.000 an error, as you should report p < 0.001. Furthermore, p < 0.03 is an error if the p-value was 0.031, and one should simply report exact p-values (p = 0.031). Statcheck might miss one-sided tests, and falsely assume the p-value is incorrect. For more information, see StatCheck.

This module only checks statistical results reported in the running text of the manuscript. It cannot (yet) process statistics reported only in tables.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 685 tests with 34 instances of inconsistent reporting, Statcheck correctly detected 34 of them, and incorrectly identified 26. Therefore 0% of true instances were missed, and 43% of detections were false positives. See https://osf.io/preprints/psyarxiv/tcxaj_v1/ for more details of the validation.

How Exact P-Values works

List any p-values reported with insufficient precision (e.g., p < .05 or p = n.s.) or reported as exactly zero (e.g., p = .000).

This module uses regular expressions to identify p-values. It will flag any values reported as p > ? or p < numbers greater than .001. It will also flag p-values reported as exactly zero (e.g., p = .000, p = 0.00), which are mathematically impossible — p-values are never exactly zero and should instead be reported as p < .001.

A p-value that is not the result of a test is not flagged: a table note (“* p < .05, ** p < .01”), a figure legend (“Asterisks indicate significant differences (p < .05)”, “Values in bold are significant at p < .05”) or a stated threshold (“p < .05 was considered significant”, “thresholded at p < .001”). GROBID often puts such notes into the running text, so each p-value is judged by the words in its own clause (the text up to a “;” or a full stop), and never left out when a test statistic belongs to it (“F(1, 7) = 8.03, # p < .05”). The column not_a_test of the table says why a p-value was left out (“marker”, “threshold” or “legend”). Notes in other forms, such as a marker after the p-value (“p < .05 (*)“), are still flagged.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (“decreased at the p < .05 significance threshold”).

This module only checks p-values reported in the running text of the manuscript. It cannot (yet) process p-values reported only in tables (as opposed to a table’s footnote text, which the module does see and tries to exclude — see above).

This module was developed by Lisa DeBruine and Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 225 papers containing 405 instances of non-exact p-values, the module correctly detected 269 cases (true positives) and incorrectly identified 78 (false positives). It missed 136 instances of imprecisely reported p-values (false negatives) and correctly identified 4557 cases of precisely reported p-values (true negative). Additionally, 78% of positive detections were correct (positive predictive value).

How Non-Significant P Value Check works

This module checks for imprecisely reported p values. If p > .05 is detected, it warns for misinterpretations.

The nonsignificant p-value check searches for regular expressions that match a predefined pattern. The module identifies all p-values in a manuscript and selects those that are not reported to be smaller than or equal to 0.05. It returns all sentences containing non-significant p-values.

In the future, the Metacheck team aims to incorporate a machine learning classifier to only return sentences likely to contain misinterpretations. If you want to help to improve the module, reach out to the Metacheck development team.

This module only checks p-values reported in the running text of the manuscript. It cannot (yet) process p-values reported only in tables.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 194 papers with 1602 instances of non-significant p-values, this module correctly detected 1486 of them, and incorrectly identified 153. Additionally, 91% of detections were true instances (positive predictive value). That is, when this module flags non-significant p-values in a paper, it correctly identifies an issue 91% of the time.

How Effect Sizes in t-tests and F-tests works

The Effect Size module checks if effect sizes are correctly reported in t-tests and F-tests.

The Effect Size check searches for regular expressions that match typical ways in which effect sizes are reported. It subsequently checks different ways in which Cohen’s d, g, ηp2, and ωp2 can be computed against the reported value. If effects are missing, or might be incorrect, you the module provides a warning. The module was validated on APA reported statistical tests, and might miss effect sizes that were reported in other reporting styles. It was validated by the Metacheck team on papers published in Psychological Science.

This module only checks statistical results reported in the running text of the manuscript. It cannot (yet) process statistics reported only in tables.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 161 papers with 1469 tests, this module correctly detected 1106 reported effect sizes (true positives) and correctly identified 295 cases where no effect size was present (true negatives). However, it missed 23 that were reported (false negatives), and incorrectly identified 45 effect sizes when none were reported (false positives). Among all instances detected by the module, 96% were true cases (positive predictive value). In a validation against 221 reported Cohen’s d effect sizes, it correctly indicated coherence in 218 cases (99%). In a validation against 485 partial eta-squared effect sizes, it correctly indicated coherence in 480 (99%)

How Codebook Check works

This module checks whether the data columns in a repository are documented in a codebook or README. It locates codebook/readme files, extracts the variable definitions they contain, matches those definitions against the data columns extracted by data_check, and reports documentation coverage: how many data columns are documented, and which documented variables are never used.

The Codebook Check module consumes the columns and file classification produced by data_check (and, transitively, repo_check). Files classified as codebook or readme are parsed with parse_codebook(), which reads structured tables (CSV/TSV/Excel with a variable-name column and a label column), embedded labels in haven files (SPSS/Stata/SAS), and plain text from rich-text formats (docx/pdf/rtf/odt). Embedded haven labels from data files are also harvested directly.

Each data column is then matched against the parsed variable definitions with match_column_labels(), using normalised-name matching with experiment-group scoping, haven-label priority, and rule-based label-equivalence merging.

Beyond the variable label, the module harvests the DDI-style per-variable properties a source supplies: the value labels / code list (the 1=“Strongly disagree”…5=“Strongly agree” mapping — from SPSS/Stata value labels and from a codebook “values”/“coding” column), the missing-value scheme (which codes denote missingness, from haven declared missings and labels that read as “refused”/“n/a”), and question text and columns when present. These are carried onto the matched data columns and exported into the Psych-DS variableMeasured (as a schema.org code list plus namespaced metacheck: fields).

The module defaults to rules-only when llm_use(FALSE). When llm_use(TRUE), three optional LLM tiers run: parsing unstructured codebook text that the rules could not handle, fuzzy-matching still-unlabelled columns to still-unmatched codebook variables, and merging conflicting label definitions into a single canonical label.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: This module has not been validated. All checks in the codebook_check module have unknown error rates. Carefully evaluate the output of this module. You can help improve this module by reporting an issue on GitHub.

How Repository Check works

This module retrieves information from repositories.

The Repository Check module lists files on the OSF, GitHub, ResearchBox, DSpace (PsychArchives and other legacy- and DSpace 7-based installations), Zenodo, Dataverse, Figshare, Dryad, ReShare, 4TU.ResearchData, Mendeley Data, DataONE (Arctic Data Center, KNB, and other member nodes), and LDbase based on links in the manuscript.

Listing a repository’s files never requires an API key, but some hosts answer faster or more completely with one: OSF allows 100 requests/hour unauthenticated versus 10,000/day with a token (see [osf_pat()]), and Dryad enforces a strict per-IP daily quota on repeated listing (see cache below). Dryad is a special case beyond rate limits: listing a Dryad dataset’s files works without a key, but actually downloading file CONTENTS from Dryad fails with HTTP 401 unless a key is set, even for a fully public dataset (see [dryad_pat()] or [dryad_auth()]). Since this module only lists files and never downloads their contents itself, that limitation applies to data_check and code_check (which do download content), not here – see their own documentation.

When a linked OSF page is a registration, its registered_from project (the one it was registered from, which the manuscript itself may never link directly) is also checked: if that project is public its files are listed under its own URL, and if it is closed or otherwise inaccessible the report flags it explicitly, since some registrations only describe their content rather than mirroring it.

If you want to extend the package to be able to download files from additional data repositories reach out to the Metacheck development team.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: This module has not been validated. All checks in the repo_check module have unknown error rates. Carefully evaluate the output of this module. You can help improve this module by reporting an issue on GitHub.

How Code Check works

This module retrieves information from repositories checked by repo_check about code files (R, Python, SAS, SPSS, Stata, Mplus, MATLAB).

The Code Check module checks R (also R Markdown and Quarto), Python (also Jupyter notebooks), SAS, SPSS, Stata, Mplus, and MATLAB files, using regular expressions to check the code; JASP files are listed but not read. The language of a Quarto document or a notebook is read from the file itself (its engine or kernel), not from its extension. The regular expression search will detect the number of comments, the lines at which libraries/imports are loaded, attempts to detect absolute paths to files, setwd() and install.packages() calls, and lists files that are loaded, and checks if these files are in the repository; R code is also parsed. The module will return suggestions to improve the code if there are no comments, if libraries/imports are loaded in lines further than 4 lines apart, if files that are loaded are not in the repository, if absolute file paths, setwd() or install.packages() are found, and if R code cannot be parsed.

The regular expressions can miss information in code files, or falsely detect parts of the code as a fixed file path. Libraries/imports might be loaded in one block, even if there are more than 3 intermittent lines. The module was tried out internally on papers published in Psychological Science, but has not been formally validated. There might be valid reasons why some loaded files can’t be shared, but the module can’t evaluate these reasons, and always gives a warning.

The module also checks whether the repository pins the R/package versions the analysis actually depended on: an renv.lock file (parsed for the R version and every locked package + its version/source), a sessionInfo()/sessioninfo::session_info() text dump (matched by filename — sessionInfo.txt/session_info.txt and similar, or embedded in a README), or a groundhog::groundhog.library()/checkpoint::checkpoint() date-pin call in the code (a bare library(groundhog)/library(checkpoint) does not count — the pinning call itself must be present). When none of these is found, the report flags it as a reproducibility gap: package versions may drift between when the analysis was run and any later reproduction attempt.

If you want to extend the package to perform additional checks on code files, or make the checks work on other types of code files, reach out to the Metacheck development team.

Checking code requires downloading its file contents. For a paper whose repository is on Dryad, this never succeeds unless a Dryad API key is set: Dryad requires one to download file bytes, even from a fully public dataset (listing the repository’s files does not need one). Without a key, every Dryad-hosted code file is listed but unchecked, and a warning naming Dryad and ?dryad_pat/?dryad_auth is included among the download failures recorded in the manifest.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Raphael Merz

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: This module has not been validated. All checks in the code_check module have unknown error rates. Carefully evaluate the output of this module. You can help improve this module by reporting an issue on GitHub.

How Data Check works

This module classifies the files in a repository into semantic types (data, codebook, code, software, output, supplemental, readme, asset, other) and, for tabular data files, extracts each column’s type and summary statistics.

The Data Check module consumes the file list produced by repo_check (or any files added via local_path). Each file is classified with rule-based heuristics layered over metacheck’s file_category() and file_types: file names matching README / codebook patterns win first, then an extension crosswalk, then format-locked extension overrides. For every file classified as tabular data that is available locally, the module reads the file head, describes each column with data_col_facets() and computes summary statistics for numeric columns. Every sheet of a spreadsheet that holds a table is read: a file with several such sheets has its columns under source_file = "file.xlsx [sheet]", and the sheet column names the sheet of any spreadsheet with several sheets; a sheet of notes or a codebook is treated as documentation when the file has another table. Following DDI, a column is described by orthogonal facets rather than a single type: representation (numeric/text/datetime/code — how it is stored), measurement_level (Stevens: nominal/ordinal/interval/ratio), concept (what it measures: reaction_time/age/gender/likert/id/…), role (identifier/measure/condition/timestamp), unit, and a quality state (ok/empty/constant). Concepts are detected by name+value rules (the demographic concepts via data_check_demographic()); when llm_use(TRUE) the model fills concepts and measurement levels the rules left blank. Qualtrics survey exports are recognised (data_check_is_qualtrics()): their extra header rows are stripped so columns type correctly, and the reserved response-metadata columns (StartDate, Duration, Finished, …) are tagged.

The module defaults to rules-only when llm_use(FALSE): columns the rules cannot resolve (ambiguous 3–20-unique integers, ambiguous character columns) fall back to continuous / text respectively. When llm_use(TRUE), ambiguous columns and unresolved file types (other) are sent to llm() for optional refinement, and every file is assigned a study group (ex1, pilot2, shared, …) so that multi-study repositories can be recognised (used by psychds_check). Without an LLM the study group is left NA (unknown).

Column extraction requires files to be readable from disk. Files fetched by repo_check from OSF/GitHub/etc. without a local copy (file_location is NA) are classified but not column-extracted; pass local_path to point at a downloaded copy of the repository.

For a paper whose repository is on Dryad, this means column extraction never happens unless a Dryad API key is set: Dryad requires one to download file bytes, even from a fully public dataset (dataset listing and metadata do not need one). Without a key, every Dryad file stays classified but un-downloaded, column_n is 0, and a warning naming Dryad and ?dryad_pat/?dryad_auth is included among the download failures. A one-time session message is also shown (see repo_check) the first time a Dryad dataset is encountered with no key set.

Every downloaded text file the authors wrote (code, settings, survey definitions such as Qualtrics .qsf files, documentation, outputs) is searched for keys: API keys, access tokens and private keys, which let anyone who downloads the file use a paid service at the authors’ cost. Of a tabular data file only the column names and first 3 rows of the table as read are searched: its values come from participants, but a key the authors set for a whole survey (as embedded data in a Qualtrics survey flow) is exported in every response. The search uses the rules of the secret scanner betterleaks (https://github.com/betterleaks/betterleaks, MIT licence) of high and medium confidence. A key found turns the traffic light red; the report and the keys table give its file, line and type, and only its beginning. Other files over 25 MB and binary files are not searched. A key is never tested with its provider. Every module’s result has any whole key replaced by “keyremoved” (see module_run()).

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: This module has not been validated. All checks in the data_check module have unknown error rates. Carefully evaluate the output of this module. You can help improve this module by reporting an issue on GitHub.

How Reproducibility Check works

This module assesses whether a paper’s R and Python code can be run on its data. It works in two phases. The static phase (always run) collects the package dependencies the code declares, rewrites the data-file paths that do not work in the repository as the authors organised it, works out the order the scripts must run in, and diagnoses why any referenced input file is unavailable — reporting what a reproduction attempt would involve and where it is likely to break. The execution phase (opt-in, execute = TRUE) then actually runs the code: it copies the repository into a throwaway directory, optionally installs the declared dependencies into a throwaway library, runs each script in order in an isolated subprocess with a per-script timeout, and captures the outcome and full output of each run.

By default (execute = FALSE) the module does not run any code — it performs only static analysis: reading dependencies with the same extractors as code_check, finding the files the code references in the repository, and building a run-order dependency graph. It reports what would be installed and run rather than doing it.

When execute = TRUE, the module additionally runs the downloaded code on your machine — a deliberate, opt-in action gated behind that argument (callr is required for R code). Each script runs in an isolated subprocess so a crash cannot take down the R session; note this isolates crashes, not the filesystem or network. Installs (when install_missing = TRUE) and the throwaway run library never touch your main R library. Each script’s outcome is one of ran_ok, errored, timed_out, dependency_unavailable, not_parsed, run_by_source (an R script another script runs with source(), which is run only inside that script, since on its own it lacks the packages and objects the sourcing script sets up first), run_by_import (a Python file other files import, a module rather than a script, unless it has an if __name__ == "__main__": block), jags_model (a JAGS or BUGS model saved with an R extension, which another script reads) or not_r_content (a file that is not R at all, such as a JSON or HTML dump); these last two are not run and are not failures. python2 marks Python 2 code that was not run. With sandbox = "docker" such code runs with Python 2.7 (option metacheck.docker_image_py2; FALSE turns this off), which modifications records; it is never converted, since that can change results. defines_functions is a file that only defines functions, which is used, not run (table$used_by names the scripts that use it), and not_analysis is a file of software rather than of the analysis: a package’s code, tests, documentation or setup.py, a copy of a tool, a web application, a script a program wrote (table$not_analysis_why says which); neither is run or counted as a script. docker_failed means the container never started, which says nothing about the script, so it keeps the light from being green but does not make it red. needs_a_person is a script that stopped because it asks a person to choose a file or answer a question, or that starts an app, and needs_internet one that stopped because the network is off in a Docker run, or, with internet = TRUE, could not reach what it asked for; download_too_large is a script stopped for downloading more than the limits allow (see internet), and out_of_memory one that, or a program it started (such as a compiler), ran out of the memory each script may use. All four are treated the same way. not_downloaded is a script that stopped on a file the repository lists but that was not downloaded, such as one over max_file_size: it could not be tried, so it is not counted as a script that did not reproduce (summary_table$repro_not_downloaded_n counts them apart). not_read is a file metacheck could not read, so it was not run; the light is then not green, as the file may read and run on another computer, and table$error_message says why, naming a package that is installed but cannot be loaded on the computer that ran the check. empty is a file with nothing in it, which is not run or counted as a script. For a script that did not run through, table$error_message is its error, short (at most 300 characters): the error line of its output, which names a package that is not there, with the address it asked for when it needed the internet, or the time limit it reached; table$reason sorts it into a kind. A timeout means “still running at the cutoff”, not a failure, so raise timeout for legitimately long-running (e.g. Bayesian) scripts. dependency_unavailable means the script’s own package could not be installed from live CRAN, the CRAN Archive, or a named GitHub/URL source — an infrastructure limitation, not a defect in the paper’s code, so unlike errored/timed_out it does not force the traffic light red. The full stdout/stderr of every run is kept in the result’s run_results (the report shows it in per-script dropdowns, capped for readability). The traffic light reflects the STATIC readiness signals by default, but an execution error (errored/timed_out) does recolour it to red — a script that crashes on its own analysis is a genuine reproduction failure. A script that fails with could not find function is run once more with the library() calls the project’s other scripts make added at its top (or the one package that exports the function, or magrittr for %>%), and a script that then runs is reported as reproducible only after that repair.

Dependencies are reported name-only, with the source (CRAN, GitHub, or a base package already shipped with R) — static analysis of the code cannot know which version was used, and running against current package versions is itself informative: a break argues the authors should have pinned versions. When the repository does record versions, a run with recorded_versions = TRUE installs the packages the scripts load at those versions, but it does not change the R version, which remains a limitation of the check.

Run order is derived from read-after-write data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads must run first), source() edges, and numeric filename prefixes as a weak tie-breaker. Ambiguous orderings, dependency cycles, and inputs a script reads but that no earlier script produces (and that are not in the repository) are surfaced as warnings, since these are the situations most likely to make an otherwise-correct reproduction fail.

Python code (.py files, and notebooks and Quarto documents whose code is Python, from which the code is extracted first) goes through the same two phases, reported in its own “Python code” section. Each file is checked for syntax errors with Python’s own parser when a Python interpreter (python, or else python3) is available; dependencies are read from the import statements, with versions from a requirements.txt or pyproject.toml when there is one, and installed with pip; each script runs as its own python process (processx is required), so unlike R scripts, a name one script defines is not available to another. When no Python interpreter is available, the Python files are reported as not run and the R results are still returned. Statistics the Python scripts print are compared with the paper together with the R output and any self-reproducible output (JASP/jamovi, SPSS-Viewer, notebook outputs).

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How PubPeer Comments works

This module checks references and warns for citations that have comments on pubpeer (excluding Statcheck comments).

The PubPeer module uses the PubPeer API to check for each reference that has a DOI whether there are comments on the post-publication peer review platform. If comments are found, a link to the comments is provided. Comments by ‘Statcheck’ on PubPeer are ignored, see https://retractionwatch.com/2016/09/02/heres-why-more-than-50000-psychology-studies-are-about-to-have-pubpeer-entries/.

The module requires that the reference has a DOI. If you run the doi_check module in a pipeline before this, it will use the enhanced DOI list from that module, otherwise it will only run on references with existing DOIs.

For more information, see PubPeer.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How RetractionWatch works

This module checks references and warns for citations in the RetractionWatch Database.

The RetractionWatch Check module compares the reference list against studies in the RetractionWatch database based on the DOI. If a study in the database is found, a reminder is provided that the study was retracted, has an expression of concern, or a correction.

The module requires that the reference has a DOI. If you run the ref_doi_check module in a pipeline before this, it will use the enhanced DOI list from that module, otherwise it will only run on references with existing DOIs.

It is possible the authors are already aware that a study was retracted, but the module can’t evaluate this.

The database can be manually updated with the rw_update function. For more information, see https://gitlab.com/crossref/retraction-watch-data.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How Replication Check works

This module checks references and warns for citations of original studies for which replication or reproduction studies exist in the FLoRA database.

The Replication Check module compares the reference list against studies in the FLoRA (FORRT Library of Replication Attempts) database based on the DOI. If a study in the database is found, a reminder is provided that a replication or reproduction of the original study exists, and should be cited (currently, a warning is provided regardless of whether the replication/reproduction study is already cited).

The module requires that the reference has a DOI. If you run the ref_doi_check module in a pipeline before this, it will use the enhanced DOI list from that module, otherwise it will only run on references with existing DOIs.

It is possible the original study was cited for other reasons than the empirical claim tested, or that the replication/reproduction in the FLoRA database is for only one of the studies in the paper, and not the study the authors discuss.

The database can be manually updated with the FLoRA_update() function. For more information, see https://forrt.org/FLoRA/.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens, Lisa DeBruine and Lukas Wallrich

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Full text

Abstract

We thank all the members of the Glimcher and Tymula labs for their valuable discussions, constructive feedback, and support throughout the project. We thank Dr.

1. Introduction

In the mid-1600s, Blaise Pascal introduced the first mathematical framework for understanding human decision-making (Pascal, 1670). He emphasized the notion that humans ought to be acting in a way that rationally and consistently maximized some objective -a mathematical representation of the goal an individual seeks to achieve through their choices. Reasoning that more of a good thing was always better than less, he concluded that the only rational objective was to maximize long-term average outcomes or returns. Humans, he argued, should simply be behaving consistently to get more of what they liked and less of what they disliked. That strategy, now called expected value theory, was used to define rational decision-making in domains ranging from religious beliefs (Pascal, 1670), to fear of accidental death, to wealth maximization (Arnauld & Nicole, 1996). Overall, Pascal's hypothesis rested on two key insights: First, that the objective value of an option is simply the product of gain (or loss) and the probability of that outcome (Pascal & Fermat, 1654). Second, that humans should rationally structure their choices to consistently pursue their goals (Pascal, 1670).

Since Pascal, choice theory has, perhaps unfortunately, undergone a series of revolutions that have shifted it away from this relatively simple and intuitive framework. The first shift was driven by the observation that humans often exhibit what is called risk-averse behavior, apparently preferring lower long-run earnings in order to minimize variance across their possible outcomes. Daniel Bernoulli recognized that this riskaversion was incompatible with most scholars' understanding of Pascal's ideas. He argued that humans act to maximize a different objective, the mathematical product of a logarithmic transformation of gain (the utility function) and the probability of receiving that gain (Bernoulli, 1738).

By the mid-20th century, the notion of what humans were trying to maximize had been relaxed even further based on new mathematical (Pareto, 1906) and theoretical-empirical (Samuelson, 1947) insights. In the expected utility theory, which emerged from these insights, the focus shifted away from the specification of a particular utility function to basic tests of whether observed choice behavior could be accounted for by any utility function at all (Samuelson, 1952; Savage, 1954; Von Neumann & Morgenstern, 1944). Scholars stopped defining what a given individual should maximize, they simply tested whether observed behavior was consistently aimed at maximizing any goal at all. By the 1970s, however, it was clear that human choices were not reliably pursuing even the most byzantine of fixed utility functions (Allais, 1953; Ellsberg, 1961). These observations led many economists and psychologists to abandon the notion that behavior was logically consistent: that behavior reflected the rational pursuit of any goal at all. Accordingly, psychologists shifted away from making statements about why humans made the choices they did, or even from making statements about what humans should choose. Instead, they shifted towards simply predicting what a given human chooser would do in a given situation. Kahneman and Tversky (Kahneman & Tversky, 1979; Tversky & Kahneman, 1981), in their seminal work defining prospect theory, laid the foundation for these purely predictive theories, abandoning logical consistency (or more formally: transitivity) in favor of descriptive power. Their model adopted a referencedependent representation of utility (formally a value function) with multiple empirically derived features and a subjective notion of probability -all of which varied significantly from individual-to-individual and context-to-context. With these components, prospect theory and its progeny did a better job of predicting what humans do choose. What the theory lacked, however, was an explanation of why people made such apparently inconsistent and undirected decisions.

Here, we employ a new approach in an effort to explain the why of many of the classes of choice behavior that Kahneman and Tversky accurately described. To accomplish this goal, we first return to the simplest possible objective: Pascal's assertion that people want to go home with as much good-stuff as possiblefoot_0 . In the spirit of Herb Simon (Simon, 1955), we acknowledge that humans have limited cognitive capacity, and that adding capacity always comes at a cost (a requirement we have shown is imposed by the laws of physics (Steverson et al., 2019)). We define cognitive capacity in the domain of human decision-making as a limit on representational precision (the entropy of the representation), capturing the notion that a given finite level of precision acts as a kind of filter which conditions our internal representation.

How does a simple expected value-like objective combine with limited precision to define optimal choice behavior? We argue that the human nervous system must, in essence, balance the costs of precision against the gains achieved by a more accurate maximization of expected value (Steverson et al., 2019). Drawing inspiration from Bayesian Theory (Bayes, 1763) and Signal Detection Theory (Green & Swets, 2000), we acknowledge that computing the tradeoff between cost and benefit when the world is imprecisely represented requires some knowledge about the structure of the choice environment (essentially a distributional Bayesian prior). We conclude that if the chooser takes as inputs a knowledge (perhaps imperfect) of the structure of the choice environment and knowledge of their own level of precision, they can use that information to select an optimal task-appropriate utility function. This kind of utility function, one selected implicitly by the brain, can be conceptualized as a tool selected by the decision-maker to sculpt their internal representation of value in a way that maximizes average earnings (or minimizes errors) given the limits of their precision. In our construction, the objective-of-choice (maximizing reward or minimizing errors) and the utility function are thus formally separated. The utility function (and the risk attitude it implies) becomes a tool used by the nervous system to achieve the simplest possible goal. Once we employ this approach, we find that many features of human choice previously thought of as irrational resolve as simple strategies for consistent maximization given the constraints imposed by physics on the human brain.

Our approach thus differs from many classical approaches in a number of ways: • We assume that the detailed probabilistic structure of the current reward environment matters to choosers.

This represents a significant departure from most mainstream theories in economics and psychology that define a choice problem as the (sometimes probabilistic) options faced by a decision-maker but leave out the likelihood with which each option is encountered. We consider the likelihood that any given option becomes available for choice to be fundamental for the meaningful specification of a choice problem. In this, we deviate from classical and neoclassical economics, requiring a different and more complete specification of the choice environment as a fundamental part of the choice problem.

• Following Pascal, we assume that a decision-maker's goal is either to 1) maximize long-run average earnings, or 2) minimize their error rates (where an error is choosing an option other than the one that maximizes earnings). Thus, we abandon the notion that humans want to minimize risk in the situations we are modeling. Risk attitudes emerge, in our approach, as a byproduct of the utility functions that choosers select to maximize their objective goals.

• Like most previous theorists, we assume that humans transform objective value inputs to subjective values using a utility-like function. Where we differ from traditional approaches is that we place that representational function under the (non-conscious) control of the chooser (either by their brain or by evolution). In the language of economics, we endogenize the utility function and separate it from their objective.

• We initially leave as a free parameter the precise level of cognitive capacity available to the chooser, examining exhaustively the optimal utility functions that emerge for choosers at any possible level of precision. In our approach, different levels of cognitive capacity are a primary source of individual variation. (A secondary source of variation arises from the subject's individually held prior about the reward distribution of the environment.) Perhaps surprisingly, we find that once the utility function is under the control of the chooser, the advantage incurred by increasing cognitive capacity (which we define formally below) is often surprisingly small. Losses produced by having low cognitive capacity can often be well-compensated for with simple changes to the utility function. In the language of economics: the returns-to-precision are less than might be expected.

• In an allied paper (Glimcher et al., 2026), we extend this set of observations and explore the notion that allocated cognitive capacity itself may also be under the control of the chooser (at least to some extent). In that extension of this work, we define the precise cost of precision and allow the chooser to optimally select how much precision to purchase before selecting a utility function. This final phase of our approach allows us to fully define human choice as an optimization problem where the only currently unmeasured parameter is the cost of precision to the decision-maker. One unique feature of this approach is that it defines the entire choice problem and specifies the utility function and the chooser's stochasticity without resorting to any free parameters in the model of theory. This approach is, in essence, a one parameter model of decision-making that can account for all of behaviors observed in prospect theory.

The work presented here, it should be noted, stops short of exploring decisions over risky lotteries. While in this paper, we view the world as probabilistic, we explore choices which arise in that probabilistic world that are always made between two certain outcomes. In the discussion section, we describe how our approach can be extended to the domain of risky choice. We wish to be explicit about this scope restriction: the theoretical framework, analytical derivations, and simulations presented in this paper apply exclusively to this class of riskless choice -although we find that many classes of puzzling behavior classically associated with risky-choice may not involve risk at all. We adopt this restriction deliberately to isolate the role of representational capacity in shaping value functions, without introducing the additional complexity of probability representation. Readers seeking a general theory of decision under risk will find that our current results, while suggestive, do not yet constitute one. Our approach, however, is extensible to the domain of risky choice and a second presentation of that set of extensions is forthcoming.

What stands out for us in this theory of decision-making amongst certain outcomes is how many puzzling phenomena become easily explainable. The sigmoidal value function of Kahneman and Tversky (Kahneman & Tversky, 1979), the concave utility function of Bernoulli (Bernoulli, 1738), and the linear utility function of Pascal (Pascal, 1670) all emerge as nested examples of rational strategies that are required of choosers who face different environments with varying degrees of precision. It is in this regard that we hope our approach has the most impact, effectively serving as a theory of why seemingly irrational behaviors and distortions from objective value-coding emerge. We note that our approach is closely related to a number of recent approaches that have inspired and shaped this work. Of particular note, our work descends from the original theory of stochastic choice pioneered by McFadden (McFadden, 1973), whose random utility framework models the probabilistic nature of observed choices by adding noise to an otherwise fixed utility function. The key difference between our framework and that of McFadden is that in his specification, the utility function and the noise distribution are both exogenous and separately specified, whereas in ours, the utility function is selected by the chooser in response to their noise level. However, like McFadden, we rely principally on an additive Gaussian noise term, although this is not required. In the Supplementary Materials we show that our findings are robust to other noise specifications, including those explored by Zhou et al., (2024) for efficient sensory encoding. In an extension of this work (Glimcher et al., 2026), we show that even the noise level, irrespective of the distributional structure of the noise, can be selected by the chooser in response to a specified cost-of-cognition -further reducing the number of free parameters required for this approach.

We focus on the two objectives of expected earnings maximization and error minimization as these represent the two most theoretically grounded and empirically motivated candidates in the literature, descending respectively from Pascal's normative benchmark and from the empirical works (Robson, 2001; Polanía et al., 2019; Woodford, 2014).

With regard to other closely related work, we note that our approach descends from efficient-coding and noisy-representation accounts of value and choice, which show that distortions in value or probability can arise as optimal adaptations to limited precision (Glimcher, 2011). In one prominent example derived from Glimcher (2011), Woodford (2014) derived stochastic choice behavior from Shannon capacity constraints under rational inattention. Polanía, Woodford & Ruff (2019) extended this approach by providing neural and behavioral evidence that the brain adapts its representational resolution to the prior distribution of experienced outcomes. Khaw, Li, & Woodford (2021) demonstrated that log-normally distributed noise in value representations produces apparent small-stakes risk aversion. Barretto-García et al. (2023) extended this to individual differences in risk attitudes. Frydman & Jin (2021) derived both utility curvature and probability weighting from efficient coding of risky lotteries. Juechems et al. (2021) derived optimal utility and probability functions for agents with finite computational precision. Heng, Woodford & Polanía (2020) showed that humans adapt their sampling behavior to environmental distributions to economize on cognitive resources.

We share with all of these papers, which descend from Glimcher (2011), the central premise that apparent distortions in value representation reflect rational adaptation to finite capacity, but innovate and consolidate to yield a single and highly tractable framework. First, we focus on riskless choice between certain outcomes before using our consolidated approach with regard to risky lotteries. This is not a trivial distinction and extending our framework to risky lotteries requires separately modelling the capacity-constrained representation of outcome probability using exactly the approach proposed here for utility. Second, and more fundamentally, these accounts derive the utility function as a fixed consequence of a specific coding problem, with a given prior and a given noise model as the universal inputs that drive our model. Our framework differs fundamentally from these earlier approaches in that for us, the utility function is the explicit variable over which the chooser optimizes. Third, rather than characterizing a single optimal function for a given prior and noise model, as in these other approaches, we exhaustively map optimal utility functions across the full space of precision levels, from near-zero to near-infinite precision, and across many reward distributions. This allows us to generate the full family of optimal functions as a continuous output and allows our approach to be used in almost any situation, rather than yielding a point solution for a particular problem of interest. We also find, for the first time, that the returns to increasing cognitive precision are surprisingly small once the utility function is optimally adjusted to the available capacity, with a doubling of encoding resources yielding only a two to three percent improvement in average earnings.

Our approach also incorporates important features of the Decision-by-Sampling literature (e.g., Stewart et al., 2006 Stewart et al., , 2015)). In that literature, Bhui & Gershman (2018) provided an important normative foundation for our general approach, showing that rank-based sampling is formally equivalent to efficient coding. Our framework also, of course, captures ideas from evolutionary and biological accounts of utility (Netzer, 2009; Netzer et al., 2025; Rayo & Becker, 2007; Robson, 2001; Robson et al., 2023). What unifies all these accounts, and what we adopt from them, is the principle that the utility function is an optimized response to the structure of the environment and the constraints under which choices are made. Our approach departs from these in that we treat the full probabilistic structure of the reward environment as a formal component of the choice problem and treat the function as both dynamic and fully endogenous to the chooser.

Finally, our work is also closely related to, and draws deep inspiration from, recent contributions that study the cognitive limits of valuation and choice, including work by Charness et al. (2013), Oprea (2024), and Webb et al. (2021). These papers collectively establish that there is substantial individual variation in the quality of utility maximization that cannot be captured by a single fixed utility function, and that cognitive limits are a primary driver of that variation. Our approach complements this literature by providing a normative account of how valuation itself should adapt to such constraints, rather than treating the resulting utility distortions as exogenous or descriptive.

2. Methods

We present our methods in two ways. In sections 2.1-2.3, we present a formal mathematical specification of the problem we set out to solve, which may not be appropriate for all readers. In section 2.4, we present a graphical overview of our methods that should be appropriate for all readers. Readers with a deep mathematical interest in our approach should read all four sections. Readers with intermediate interest are encouraged to skip sections 2.2 and 2.3. Readers interested in the general approach should proceed directly to section 2.4.

It is also important to note that in attempting to answer the larger question: What is the optimal utility function for a given environment when facing a riskless choice problem, we have developed three overlapping mathematical approaches. We have developed a proof-based approach, an analytic approach that relies on features of Gaussian noise to achieve computational simplicity, and a general-purpose Monte Carlo-based approach which can solve essentially any choice problem. The latter two approaches are described in this paper. Interested readers can examine the proof-based approach in an adjacent economicsstyle paper, which is partially overlapping in content but aimed at an economics audience (Glimcher et al., 2026). The analytic approach generalizes that purely mathematical solution to environments in which choosers face a larger number of possible reward values 2 . The bulk of the material presented here relies on this analytic approach. This analytic approach, however, cannot be used to identify an optimal utility function when the decision-maker must choose between more than two options (a change which has a significant impact on the shape of the optimal utility function). For that class of problems, we generalize our solution to a numerical Monte-Carlo-style strategy (Metropolis & Ulam, 1949). This allows us to solve for optimal utility functions under essentially any conditions.

2.1 General Mathematical Assumptions About the Choice Environment

We begin by stating explicitly the objective of the chooser is either to 1) maximize average earnings or 2) minimize the number of errors. Our goal is to recover an optimal utility function 𝑢(𝑥), which is dependent on the choice environment 3 and the cognitive capacity of the chooser, and which maximizes the stated objective function.

The choice environment is defined by a formal set containing a fixed number, 𝑚, of possible rewards (or punishments) which we call 𝑋 = {𝑥 ! , . . . , 𝑥 " }, where each 𝑥 # is a real number (a possible reward value that the decision-maker can encounter). Without loss of generality, but to make the problem more intuitive for this presentation, we assume that 𝑥 ! ≤ 𝑥 $ ≤. .. ≤ 𝑥 " (thus 𝑥 " is always used to label the largest possible reward and 𝑥 ! the smallest). Additionally, we assume that each next reward in 𝑋 increases in objective value by the same increment, for example, by one dollar.

Choice sets are constructed by drawing one or more possible rewards from the set 𝑋. A decision-maker's task is to select one option from a given choice set. The probability that any given reward will be drawn from the environment (𝑋) into a choice set with 𝑛 possible rewards is specified by a probability distribution 4.

2.1.1 Capacity Constraints on Utility

To capture the notion that humans have limited representational capacity, we follow classical psychophysics and modern economics (Fechner, 1948; Glimcher, 2011; McFadden, 1973; Simon, 1955; 2 In Glimcher, Sinha and Tymula (Glimcher et al., 2026), we also present this analytic approach, but there tie it explicitly to the closed-form proof without examining the error-minimizing objective function. The closed-form proof method and the analytic method yield identical results where they can both be applied. 3 Here, the notion of a choice environment is synonymous with a formal mathematical specification of traditional notion of a choice context. 4 For the purposes of our analytic solution, we require that the options in the choice set be i.i.d drawn from the environmental set according to the probability distribution. Our Monte-Carlo approach relaxes that constraint and allows any possible form of nonindependence including discrete covariance structures of the kind we have studied previously (e.g., Bucher & Brandenburger, 2022) and which are on occasion employed in psychological experiments.

Weber, 1846) by assuming that the decision maker has a noisy internal representation of the true value of the rewards. Decision makers decide by selecting the reward with the highest noisy utility out of all rewards in the choice set. This is thus a standard psychophysical specification of the utility function contaminated by Gaussian noise. Formally, the noisy utility of each reward 𝑥 # is defined as: where 𝑈 stands for the noisy utility, 𝑢 is the noiseless utility, and 𝜀 is 'brain' noise drawn from a normal distribution with mean zero and standard deviation of 𝜎 (𝜀~𝑁(0, 𝜎 $ )).

The capacity constraints are a direct result of the utility 𝑈 being noisy and 𝑢 being bounded, as explained below.

Following Pascal, Bernoulli, Samuelson, and von Neumann-Morgenstern (Bernoulli, 1738; Pascal, 1670; Samuelson, 1952; Von Neumann & Morgenstern, 1944), we assume for all our approaches that the noiseless utility function that maps objective rewards into their subjective valuations is weakly monotonic, i.e. 𝑢(𝑥 ! ) ≤ 𝑢(𝑥 $ ) ≤. .. ≤ 𝑢(𝑥 " ). This assumption captures the standard more-is-never-worse-than-less principle. As rewards increase in objective value, their assigned utility should stay the same or increase but can never decreasefoot_1 . We adopt weak rather than strict monotonicity to allow for the possibility that a decision-maker is indifferent between two reward levels, that is, that two objectively different rewards may be assigned the same subjective utility. We also assume that the utility function u is bounded between 0 and 1 (i.e.0 ≤ 𝑢(𝑥 ! ) ≤ 𝑢(𝑥 $ ) ≤. .. ≤ 𝑢(𝑥 " ) ≤ 1), such that there is a maximum possible level of utility a person can experience. Restricting the utility function so that it cannot have an infinite range goes against a feature of many standard economic models (e.g., Bernoulli, 1738) but anchors our theory to the physical world the human nervous system occupies and is a fundamental constraint on our theory. Together, these two assumptions define the candidate set of utility functions considered throughout this paper. No further parametric restrictions are imposed, and we do not assume any functional form, such as power utility or logarithmic utility. The optimal utility function 𝑢 * is identified by searching exhaustively over this entire candidate set, making our approach, uniquely, nonparametric with respect to the shape of the utility function.

Note that we adopt the convention that a capital 𝑈 calls out the noise-contaminated form of noisy utility while u calls out the noiseless, or mean, utility function. Our approach can be generalized to other patterns of noise (such as Weber-style multiplicative noise terms), but we begin with this simpler specification which can be tied to our formal proof that requires an additive noise term (Glimcher et al., 2026). To further demonstrate this generalizability and examine the interpretation of capacity and its dependence on the assumed noise structure, we provide additional analyses in the Supplementary Materials, examining an alternative noise specification, a more neurobiologically plausible Poisson noise structure, using both an analytical solution we derive and Monte Carlo simulations. These analyses demonstrate the robustness of our conclusions and show how the formal definition of capacity changes under this alternative specification while the underlying signal-to-noise interpretations remain intact (see Section A in the Supplementary Materials). Following the standard psychophysical convention, the magnitude of this internal noise serves as a formal metric for specifying the precision of the subjective representation of value (higher noise indicating lower precision).

To illustrate the general problem imposed by varying the levels of noise in a chooser's utility function, Figure 1A illustrates an example utility function with two different noise levels: high (𝜎 '#(' = 0.2) in green and low (𝜎 )*+ = 0.1) in blue. These will be familiar to psychologists as Weber-Fechner-style (Fechner, 1948; Weber, 1846) functions for utility (Glimcher, 2011). Like all utility functions, every point on the utility curve transforms the objective value of a reward 𝑥 # to its utility, here plus or minus noise. Since the utility of a given 𝑥 # is perturbed by noise, the distributions drawn along the y-axis represent the distribution of possible noisy utility signals 𝑈 that could be produced in response to rewards 𝑥 ! and 𝑥 $ . The probability that 𝑈(𝑥 ! ) > 𝑈(𝑥 $ ) despite the fact that 𝑥 $ > 𝑥 ! , reflects the likelihood of a noise-induced error. vertical axis has been rescaled to highlight the noisy chooser's capacity with the maximal capacity in units of standard deviation shown circled at the top of the axis. Panel C: The same rescaling, but this time for a lower-capacity chooser.

To standardize this representation and allow more direct comparison across choosers with different levels of precision, we express utility in units of representational noise. In the additive Gaussian noise model, where noise is fixed across the utility range, this amounts to rescaling the bounded utility function by its standard deviation. We apply a transformation to the utility by redefining the units of utility as capacity with an upper bound of 𝑢(𝑥) at 𝑐 (the maximum capacity of a given chooser) as:

After this rescaling, the range of the y-axis (from 0 to 𝑐) captures the capacity of the chooser, measured in the number of standard deviations which that chooser can employ for reward encoding. In this representation, high-capacity (low-noise) choosers have utility functions that span more standard deviations and low-capacity choosers have utility functions that span fewer standard deviations. This transformation has the benefit of effectively recasting the utility space into a natural unit of standard deviations, allowing direct comparison between choosers of different precision (a transformation first suggested by McFadden, (1973)). We illustrate this in the following way: In Figure 1B, where 𝜎 = 0.1, the maximum 𝑢(𝑥) = 10, the smaller overlap leads to improved discriminability between options, thereby reducing errors. In Figure 1C where 𝜎 = 0.2, the maximum 𝑢(𝑥) = 5, the larger overlap between Gaussians indicates a higher chance of making errors.

More generally, we use the term capacity to refer to the effective signal-to-noise structure of the internal representation, the extent to which differences in the utility of two or more options can be reliably distinguished given the noise embedded in the representation. The precise mathematical definition of capacity is therefore model-dependent. In the Gaussian case considered in this section, it is naturally expressed as the inverse of a fixed noise parameter, whereas under the alternative noise structure presented in the Supplementary Materials (Poisson-like variability), capacity corresponds more closely to the overall scaling of the utility function.

For simplicity and because the analytical results that follow here have an additive Gaussian noise structure, in the remainder of the paper, we represent all choosers with regard to their maximum capacity in units of standard deviation, 𝜎, which we take to be the natural units of utility under this specification.

2.2 Finding the Optimal Utility Function Analytically 6 : A solution for choices between two options

In this section, we present our analytical mathematical approach to derive the optimal utility function. (A graphical presentation of this approach can be found below in section 2.4 which may be of greater interest for many readers who might choose to skip ahead to that section.) This approach requires the following simplifications, two of which can be relaxed in the next section: 1) That the utility axis is discrete rather than continuous. 2) That choosers must select from only two options on a given trial. 3) That the choice options be drawn i.i.d. from the environment. For this first example, we choose an environment in which rewards can take a maximum of four discrete values.

2.2.1 Boundary Conditions

Any efficient decision-maker will necessarily make use of the whole range of utilities that are available to them. Therefore, they will always set the utility of the smallest possible reward value to 0 and the utility of the highest possible reward value to 𝑐 (thus 𝑢(𝑥 ! ) = 0 and 𝑢(𝑥 " ) = 𝑐). (A chooser who uses less than the full range can be trivially characterized as having a lower capacity 𝑐.)

2.2.2 Defining the Probability of Choice Errors (Error Rates)

Our first step is to define mathematically how often an error occurs when a decision maker chooses from a binary choice set using a given utility function. Consider a choice set consisting of two rewards, 𝑥 # and 𝑥 , , drawn from our set of possible rewards where 𝑥 , has the higher objective value, 𝑥 , > 𝑥 # . Their associated noisy utilities are given by 𝑈(𝑥 # ) = 𝑢(𝑥 # ) + 𝜀 # and 𝑈(𝑥 , ) = 𝑢(𝑥 , ) + 𝜀 , . The noise levels are drawn independently from a Gaussian distribution with mean 0 and a standard deviation of 𝜎 (𝜀 # , 𝜀 , ~𝑁(0, 𝜎 $ )), as seen in Figure 2A for 𝜎 = 𝟏. We use the Error rate to refer to the probability of making an error; erroneously choosing the lower-valued option 𝑥 # instead 𝑥 , . This simple algebra shows that choosers make errors when the difference between the two noise elements overwhelms the difference in the mean value of the two utilities 𝑢. Since both 𝜀 # and 𝜀 , are independently drawn from a Gaussian distribution 𝑁(0, 𝜎 $ ), the distribution of possible differences between the two will be definitionally drawn from a Gaussian distribution with mean 𝜇 # -𝜇 , and standard deviation of

To resolve this to a single probability -the probability of an error under these specific conditions -we use the complementary cumulative distribution function (CCDF) of the standard normal distribution. As illustrated graphically in Figure 2C, this corresponds to the area under the standard normal curve to the right of the threshold (colored in red) for 𝜎 = 1, the integral of which captures the net probability of an error under these specific conditions.

Therefore, the total probability of an error, given a choice between 𝑥 # and 𝑥 , where, 𝑥 , > 𝑥 # and a utility function 𝑈(𝑥) is employed, is given by the complementary cumulative distribution function of the standard normal distribution with a threshold of .

To capture the changing impact of different levels of internal noise (and hence by definition different cognitive capacities in the decision-maker), we vary the standard deviation of noise. Increasing the standard deviation (𝜎), reduces maximum capacity (𝑐) and increases the error rate. Conversely, a decrease in the standard deviation (𝜎), increases maximum capacity 𝑐, and reduces error rate because the distance between the means of the corresponding Gaussians (in units of standard deviation) is larger on the Capacity axis.

2.2.3 Finding the Optimal Utility Function

Knowing how to recover the probability of an error for any specific choice between two options for any utility function at any given capacity, we can proceed to calculate the overall earnings (gains or losses) and error rates associated with any particular utility function in any given environment. We accomplish this in two stages. First, for each choice set under a given utility function, we calculate the probability of an error as well as expected earnings. Then, after we calculate this for all possible choice pairs, we total up the aggregate errors and earnings while taking into account how often each choice set is encountered in the given environment. Below, we formally describe this process for our two optimality criteria: (1) maximizing earnings and (2) minimizing the number of errors.

2.2.3.1 Maximizing the Rewards

We start by determining the expected earnings that any given utility function delivers for a chooser with a given capacity. As before, the chooser is tasked with selecting one option from a binary choice-set, {𝑥 # , 𝑥 , } where 𝑥 , > 𝑥 # . A chooser who has no capacity constraints (no noise in their utility) would maximize their earnings by consistently choosing the higher-value option 𝑥 , . Given that there is noise in the utility function 𝑈, the chooser will sometimes choose 𝑥 # and sometimes 𝑥 , . We can use the probability of making an error (𝑃(𝑈(𝑥 # ) > 𝑈(𝑥 , )) under a given utility 𝑈 as:

Here, the expression 𝑥 # * 𝑃(𝑈(𝑥 # ) > 𝑈(𝑥 , )) represents the reward received when an error is made (when the chooser picks 𝑥 # ) multiplied by the probability with which this error happens 𝑃(𝑈(𝑥 # ) > 𝑈(𝑥 , )). The second term 𝑥 , * (1 -𝑃(𝑈(𝑥 # ) > 𝑈D𝑥 , E) represents the reward received when the correct decision is made, choosing 𝑥 , , which happens with the remaining probability. Note that while the decision is made based on noisy subjective utility 𝑈(𝑥 # ), the earnings that are maximized are always measured in units of objective reward value, the actual dollar amounts 𝑥 # and 𝑥 , , not expressed in subjective and internal utility units. This separation between the currency of decision-making and the currency of evaluation is fundamental to our framework. The utility function determines how the decision is made, but the quality of that decision is evaluated by what is received, a quantity the chooser is actually trying to maximize.

To calculate the overall expected earnings for a given utility function 𝑈, we aggregate the earnings from all possible choice sets, weighted by their respective probabilities of occurrence 𝑃({𝑥 # , 𝑥 , }).

This allows us to calculate the expected earnings for any given utility function 𝑢 with a capacity constraint (noise) specified by 𝜎. We compare the expected earnings of all these candidate utility functions {𝑢 ! , 𝑢 $ , . . . , 𝑢 ) } and label the one with the highest earnings as optimal with respect to expected earnings:

2.2.3.2 Minimizing the Number of Errors
