An alternative approach is to define optimal utility as the utility function that minimized the number of errors made by the decision-maker, regardless of the earnings loss associated with those errors. Under this criterion, the optimal utility function 𝑢 * is the one that leads to the fewest incorrect choices across all choice sets. These two approaches are importantly distinct. When maximizing rewards, making an error when choosing between an objective value of 1 and an objective value of 4 is much worse than making an error when choosing between values of 3 and 4. When minimizing errors, these two erroneous choices have equal impact on the optimization problem.

When minimizing errors is the chooser's goal, the error for a given choice set {𝑥 # , 𝑥 , } where 𝑥 , > 𝑥 # is simply the probability of incorrectly selecting the lower-value option:

To compute the total number of errors associated with a utility function u, we aggregate the errors across all possible choice sets {𝑥 # , 𝑥 , }, where 𝑥 , > 𝑥 # and 𝑥 # , 𝑥 , ∈ 𝑋 = {𝑥 ! , . . . , 𝑥 " }, weighted by their probability of encounter 𝑃({𝑥 # , 𝑥 , }):

Finally, to identify the optimal utility function from a set of 𝑙 candidate functions {𝑢 ! , 𝑢 $ , . . . , 𝑢 ) }, we select the one that minimizes the total error:

2.3 A Monte-Carlo Approach: Choices between more than two options

The analytic approach described above can be used to identify optimal utility functions when the choice sets (the options being compared) contain only two options with rewards independently drawn from the environment (where the environment is defined by the set X and its attendant probabilities of occurrence).

The key limitation of this approach is that the exact probability of correctly identifying the best option relies on the closed-form properties of the difference of two independent Gaussian random variables (a difference which is described by a Gaussian). When decision-makers must choose between more than two options or choice sets have complex covariance structures that make the rewards non-independent, this specific closed-form expression is no longer available, and the error probability cannot be derived analytically in the same tractable way. For those choice conditions, we use a Monte-Carlo-style simulation to identify the optimal utility function.

As with our analytic solution, we begin by specifying the choice environment and the capacity of the chooser (the level of internal noise). As before, the utilities for the lowest reward value and the highest reward value are set to 0 and 𝑐, respectively. As before, we generate a list of all utility functions we wish to consider: {𝑢 ! , 𝑢 $ , . . . , 𝑢 ) }. Next, for each 𝑢, we simulate one million choices and calculate either the earnings (for the reward maximization objective) or the number of errors (for the number of error minimization objective) across these simulated choices.

Our procedure is as follows: We assume a candidate utility, 𝑢 # , and a capacity level, 𝑐. Next, we draw one million choice sets (choice problems) according to the environmental reward probability structure. Then, one choice set at a time, we assign a noisy utility to each reward in this choice set following 𝑈(𝑥 # ) = 𝑢(𝑥 # ) + 𝜀 # . Then, the algorithm selects from this choice set the reward with the highest noisy utility 𝑈.

After doing this for one million choice sets, we compute the average earnings and the total number of errors for the assumed 𝑢 # with capacity level 𝑐. Finally, to identify the optimal utility function, we select the one that maximizes expected reward or minimizes the total error.

2.4 Graphical Presentation of Methods

In this section, we graphically present our Analytic and Monte-Carlo approaches to identifying an optimal utility function for a given environment for a chooser of a given capacity. Recall that our analytic method can identify an optimal utility function for environments in which 1) the decision-maker only encounters choices between two options, and 2) those two options are drawn from the set of possible options independently. Our Monte-Carlo approach, presented next, allows for more complex problems.

2.4.1 Analytic Method

We begin by describing how we identify the utility function that maximizes average reward. Consider a choice environment in which there are four possible rewards (𝑚 = 4): 𝑋 = {1,2,3,4} out of which two are randomly drawn to produce a two-option choice set. Figure 3A shows the four possible rewards on the lower axis and the bars indicate the probability that any single reward will be drawn into the choice set. This probability distribution 𝑃 for the environment defines how likely the chooser is to face each alternative from the set X, and in this example 𝑃 = {0.5,0.3,0.15,0.05}. There are thus ten possible binary choice sets that a chooser can encounter: {1,1}, {1,2}, {1,3}, {1,4}, {2,2}, {2,3}, {2,4}, {3,3}, {3,4}, and {4,4}. Figure 3B illustrates one possible choice set, {1,2}, randomly drawn from this environment.

For this example chooser, we assume that the maximum capacity 𝑐 = 3𝑆𝐷. Since the utilities of the lowest and highest reward are already set, 𝑢(1) = 0 & 𝑢(4) = 𝑐 = 3𝑆𝐷, what is left is to determine the optimal y-values for 𝑢(2) and 𝑢(3), shown as the movable points 𝑌 $ and 𝑌 : in the figure. In Figure 3C, we illustrate with gray lines a selection of example utility functions in this space. The marginal distributions projected just to the left of the y-axis show, for example straight-line utility function, how x-values of 1, 2, 3 and 4 would be transformed into noisy distributions by this chooser who has a cognitive capacity defined as spanning 3 standard deviations of representational magnitude.

Figure 3D represents how this example straight-line utility function would transform the particular choice problem shown in Figure 3B. The distributions projected just to the left of the y-axis show the resulting distribution of possible internal representations, where it is the overlap of these distributions that leads to errors, as presented in detail in sections 2.1 and 2.2. Since we want to examine a non-infinite number of possible utility functions, we make an important simplification. We restrict the set of possible utility values for 𝑢(2) and 𝑢(3) to range from 0 to 3 in 0.1 unit steps, imposing discreteness on our set of possible utility functions. This is equivalent to saying that the combination of all possible 𝑢(2) and 𝑢(3) values, and hence all allowable utility functions, can be represented as a discrete matrix, where each point in the matrix corresponds to a different potential utility function (Figure 3E). (Note that the gray region in Figure 3E corresponds to situations in which 𝑢(3) < 𝑢(2), a violation of the more-is-never-worse-than-less rule. These are places in which the optimal utility function cannot be located.) This leads to 496 possible utility functions, with two examples (a concave and convex utility) illustrated in Figure 3F and Figure 3G.

Using the algorithm described above, which renders the average reward earned by using each utility function directly computable, we can plot in color the specific earnings for any utility function specified by its 𝑌 $ and 𝑌 : values. The task of identifying the optimal utility function is now simply identifying the point in that space that yields the highest average return. The insets highlight where two example utility functions are represented in this space with their associated distributions. As one can see, for a chooser with this cognitive capacity encountering this environment, the utility functions lying towards the top right corner of Figure 3E yield the highest possible earnings. The single utility function with the highest return, for this choice environment and for a chooser with a cognitive capacity 𝑐 = 3𝑆𝐷 is highlighted with an x. To analyze the effect of changing capacities, we look for maximum reward utility functions and minimum error utility functions (see results) for a range of different cognitive capacities, 𝑐, varying from 2 to 10𝑆𝐷.

2.4.2 Effects of Varying Capacity

We then consolidate the optimal utility functions to compare the effect of increasing or decreasing capacities on the shape of the utility function. Here, the choice environment depicted in Figure 4A follows a uniform distribution 𝑃 = {0.25,0.25,0.25,0.25}. Figure 4B presents the payoff space measured across varying maximum capacity levels: 𝑐 = {2,4,6,8}. Figure 4C displays the corresponding reward maximization functions for each capacity level, while Figure 4D consolidates these curves into a single visualization, providing a comparative overview of how the function evolves with capacity expansion.

2.4.3 Generalization to More Possible Reward Values: 𝑚 > 4

To investigate the impact of increasing the environmental set size (adding more possible x-values to the utility function) while keeping the choice set fixed as a two-option problem, we extend our numerical analysis to an example where 𝑚 = 6 and the possible rewards are {1,2,3,4,5,6}. This gives us twenty-one possible binary choice sets. Following the conventions in Figure 3, Figure 5 illustrates the underlying environmental probabilities 𝑃 = {0.3,0.23,0.18,0.14,0.1,0.05} (Figure 5A) and one possible choice set {3,5}, randomly drawn from the choice environment (Figure 5B).

For this example, we assume that 𝑐 = 2𝑆𝐷. Our boundary conditions and the assumption of weak monotonicity of 𝑢 imply that 𝑢(1) =0 ≤ 𝑢(2) ≤ 𝑢(3) ≤ 𝑢(4) ≤ 𝑢(5) ≤ 𝑢(6) = 2𝑆𝐷. In Figure 5C, we illustrate with gray lines a selection of possible utilities, and in Figure 5D, one possible 𝑢(𝑥) with its associated probability of making an error in the choice set {3,5}.

We restrict the range of possible utility values for 𝑢(2), 𝑢(3), 𝑢(4) and 𝑢(5) to be from 0 to 2 in 0.1 unit steps. The combination of all allowed utility values can be represented as a 4D matrix of dimension (21, 21, 21, 21), where each point in the matrix corresponds to a different potential utility function (see Figure 5E which collapses the 4D matrix to the standard tesseract representation), although much of that matrix (the 'top left' hemi-tesseract) includes points which violate monotonicity and which we can ignore because they cannot maximize earnings or minimize errors. This leads to 10,626 possible utility functions, with two examples (a concave and convex utility) illustrated in Figures 5F and 5G. We identify from this set the reward-maximizing and the error-minimizing functions. To analyze the effect of changing capacities, we run both of these exercises for a range of different 𝑐 values from 2 to 10 SD.

2.4.4 Generalization to Larger Choice-sets with Monte-Carlo

In the preceding sections, we restricted our analysis to binary choice sets -choices between two options.

To generalize the framework, we extend our investigation to larger choice sets; situations in which a decision maker must choose amongst three or more options. This class of optimization problem is too complex to solve using the analytical method used in the preceding section. We therefore use a Monte-Carlo simulation. By simulating millions of choices drawn randomly according to the stated probability distribution for the environment, we can obtain approximations of optimal utility structures under these more complex conditions. (To validate this methodology, we show that it replicates the results obtained from the analytical example above in the Supplementary Materials.)

As before, we define the environment by a finite set of possible rewards 𝑋 = {1,2,3,4} and a probability distribution 𝑃 = {0.5,0.3,0.15,0.05} that determines how likely the chooser is to face each alternative from the set (Figure 6A). Figure 6B shows the distributions associated with 4 randomly drawn choice sets offering 3-options. For this example, we set the maximum capacity equal to 3 (𝑐 = 3𝑆𝐷). Our boundary conditions and the assumption of weak monotonicity of 𝑢 imply that 𝑢(1) =0 ≤ 𝑢(2) ≤ 𝑢(3) ≤ 𝑢(4) = 3𝑆𝐷. We restrict the range of possible utility values for 𝑢(2) and 𝑢(3) to range from 0 to 3, using 50 bins for each, resulting in a grid of candidate utility functions. For each candidate utility function 𝑢(𝑥), we randomly draw 1,000,000 choice problems and calculate average earnings and error rates (Figure 6C). To determine which prize is chosen from the choice problem presented to the chooser, we add Gaussian noise with mean 0 and standard deviation of 1 (𝜀~𝑁(0,1)) to 𝑢(𝑥) and the simulated chooser picks the option with the highest 𝑈(𝑥). The result is a map of the payoff space, which is slightly less smooth than the analytically derived space due to the stochastic nature of the simulations (Figure 6D). Two examples (a concave and convex utility) can be seen in Figures 6E and 6F.

The code behind all simulations is available at GitHub https://github.com/ShreyaSinha14468/Rationally_Selected_Utility. This study was not preregistered.

3. Results

>Results

3.1 Result I: Reward Distributions Determine Optimal Utility

Here we present the main findings of our approach. For a reader interested in our methodology, there are two parallel descriptions presented in the Methods section. Sections 2.1 to 2.3 provide a complete mathematical description of our approach. Section 2.4 provides an overview of our mathematical approach using a more graphical presentation, which will be sufficient for many readers.

We begin by examining the impact of the environmental distribution of reward on the shape of the optimal utility function. Figure 7 presents three distinct choice environments and the corresponding optimal utility functions 𝑢 * that maximize earnings and minimize errors under a capacity constraint of 𝑐 = 3𝑆𝐷. The cognitive capacity of the chooser is defined in units of standard deviation, with high numbers indicating high cognitive capacity (lower internal noise). Here, we examine optimal utilities when the decision-maker chooses between two options which are independently drawn from the probability distributions represented at the top of the figure. For more details on these features, see the Methods section.

In the top row of Figure 7A-C, each panel represents a different choice distribution with four possible options {1,2,3,4}, characterized by the probability of encountering each option: • Figure 7A -Positively Skewed Distribution: The probability of an option appearing in the choice set is inversely related to its objective value and lower-value options are more frequently encountered.

The specified environment is defined as: 𝑃 = {0.5,0.3,0.15,0.05} • Figure 7B -Uniform Distribution: All options appear with equal probability, resulting in a uniform probability distribution. The specified environment is defined as: 𝑃 = {0.25,0.25,0.25,0.25} • Figure 7C -Negatively Skewed Distribution: The probability of an option appearing in the choice set increases with objective value; high-value options are encountered more frequently. The specified environment is defined as: 𝑃 = {0.05,0.15,0.3,0.5}

The second row of Figure 7 depicts the relationship between payoffs (long-run expected earnings) and varying utility functions across the three choice environments. The heatmaps in Figure 7 D, E, F (left) illustrate how payoffs vary across all possible utility functions, within each environmental context. Warmer colors indicate higher expected earnings. We identify the bin corresponding to the highest expected earnings in each payoff space with a circle. The optimal utility function 𝑢 * associated with this bin is defined as the Reward Maximization Function and can be seen in the respective panels, Figure 7 D, E, F (right).

Note that despite the chooser's consistent objective, to maximize total earnings, the resulting optimal utility functions, 𝑢 * , exhibit systematic variations across choice environments: • In the case of a positively skewed environment, 𝑢 * is concave, consistent with Bernoulli-like riskaversion.

When low-valued rewards are most common, limited capacity choosers maximize their average rate-of-return by adopting utility functions that would be classically described as riskaverse. They do this because they are attempting to maximize their ability to discriminate between the more commonly available low-value options. We note that the original utility function proposed by Bernoulli (Bernoulli, 1738) took essentially this form and the choice problem he was trying to explain (the St Petersburg Paradox) had a positively skewed distribution of possible rewards, just as this example. This may suggest that Bernoulli's utility function would be optimal for a chooser trying to maximize reward in the St Petersburg game environment, with the caveat that the classic game explicitly involves risk which is not directly modeled here.

• When all options are equally probable, in a uniformly distributed environment, 𝑢 * is sigmoidal, suggesting an adaptive balance between what might be classically described as risk-aversion and risk-seeking behavior. The function exhibits greater sensitivity to mid-range values, ensuring efficient differentiation across the entire value spectrum which minimizes the most-costly mistakes, erroneously selecting 𝑥 ! or 𝑥 $ when 𝑥 ; is available. We note that the original sigmoidal utility function of Kahneman and Tversky was largely developed to account for behavioral data from experiments in which the probabilities of encountering a given reward were uniformly distributed. The prospect theory utility function developed for risky choice, although quite different from Bernoulli's function, might be seen as an optimal strategy for maximizing reward, this time in an experimental psychology laboratory.

• In a negatively skewed environment, 𝑢 * is convex, which would imply risk-seeking behavior where lotteries are employed, a strategy that prioritizes differentiation among common high-value options. Thus, a convex utility can, under some conditions, be optimal. This stands in stark contrast to the standard economic conclusion that such functions, at least in the domain of risky-choice, are considered irrational because they violate second-order stochastic dominance.

The third row of Figure 7 presents different utility functions for each environment, now derived under the objective of error minimization. The error space quantifies rates of decision errors for different utility functions as color. In the heatmaps in Figure 7 G, H, I (left) each bin denotes a distinct utility function, and the corresponding errors associated with it, with darker green regions indicating lower error rates. The optimal utility function, 𝑢 * , is the one that minimizes error across the entire space, the Error Minimization Function, Figure 7 G, H, I (right).

These functions also exhibit variation across different choice environments. Note that they, perhaps surprisingly, closely resemble the reward maximization functions, with only slight differences in curvature.

As we show below, there are environmental distributions which do discriminate dramatically between these two objectives, but these commonly employed environments are poorly suited to making this comparison.

3.2 Result II: Capacity Determines Utility and Earnings

Figure 8 presents three distinct choice environments along with their corresponding optimal utility functions, 𝑢 * , which maximize earnings for nine different capacity constraints varying from 2 to 10 in steps of 1. The figure also depicts how the associated payoffs for these functions change as capacity increases.

In the first column of Figure 8 (A, D and G), each panel represents a different choice distribution consisting of four possible options, {1,2,3,4}, defined by the probability of occurrence within a binary choice set. The three choice environments remain consistent with previous analyses: • Positively skewed distribution: 𝑃 = {0.5,0.3,0.15,0.05} • Uniform distribution: 𝑃 = {0.25,0.25,0.25,0.25} • Negatively skewed distribution: 𝑃 = {0.05,0.15,0.3,0.5} If we examine the second column of Figure 8, distinct utility functions emerge as capacity varies.

For low capacities: In a positively skewed environment, 𝑢 * exhibits a starkly concave shape. This would be classically viewed as implying risk aversion and a strategy that prioritizes differentiation among lowervalue options. In a uniformly distributed choice environment 𝑢 * follows the classical S-shaped form, indicating sensitivity to mid-range values. In a negatively skewed environment 𝑢 * takes a convex shape, improving discrimination amongst common highly valued rewards.

As capacity increases, however, 𝑢 * in each environment progressively approaches a linear form. This transition suggests that with higher levels of capacity, when the system can encode reward values more precisely, the need for nonlinear transformations that prioritize differentiation among specific ranges is reduced.

The right-most panels show the average rates-of-return for each of these cognitive capacity levels, in each of these environments. We plot them as a percent improvement over the rate-of-return achieved by a fully random chooser (one with zero cognitive capacity). What stands out from these data is that a two standard deviation chooser does much better than a random chooser. Adding a third standard deviation of capacity yields significant but diminishing returns. The 'returns-for-capacity,' however, decline quite quickly. Consider a chooser with 4 standard deviations of noise versus a chooser with 8 standard deviations of noise.

Neurobiologically, this might be thought of as equivalent to doubling the number of neurons encoding the utility function. In this case, a doubling of the number of neurons (or alternatively, perhaps doubling the number of possible action potentials) yields only a 2-3% increase in overall gains. For a decision-maker who can set their own utility function, it might not make much sense to spend a lot of metabolic energy creating additional cognitive capacity if it achieves very little additional gain. To examine how different goals influence the curvature of the optimal utility functions, we next repeated this analysis for a chooser trying to minimize the number of errors that they make, rather than maximizing their average rate-of-return. Figure 9 plots the results of this analysis using the same strategies as in Figure 8. When examining the optimal utility functions for these three environments, we see that they are quite similar to those observed when maximizing reward. The third column of Figure 9 (C, F, and I) illustrates the percentage of errors at varying capacity levels. Note that the error rates as a function of capacity decline more gradually than the average earnings (Figure 8 C, F, I) grew. The marginal value of increasing capacity, in some sense, is higher for an error-minimizing chooser than for a reward-maximizing chooser.

Figure 9: Following the conventions in Figure 8, we plot optimal utility functions for choosers minimizing the average number of errors that they make rather than maximizing average rates of reward (as in Figure 8). Note that the functions in the middle column are very similar to those observed for reward maximization. The right-most column plots how error rates change as capacity increases as a percent-increase over the random chooser. Notice that error rates decline quite dramatically over the first 6-8 standard deviations.

3.3 Result III: Bigger Environments Yield Steeper Sigmoids

To gain further insight into how increasing the number of possible rewards impacts 𝑢 * , we repeat our exercise for 6 reward levels.

First, we turn to reward maximization, as seen in the second column of Figure 10. With an expanded set of possible rewards, we observe the consistent emergence of an S-shaped 𝑢 * as the optimal function across all choice environments, when capacity is low. This pattern is not limited to the uniform distribution but can also be seen in positively and negatively skewed environments for very low-capacity choosers.

As capacity increases in a positively skewed environment, 𝑢 * transitions from an S-shaped form to a concave function and eventually approaches a linear form as capacity grows. In a uniformly distributed environment, the S-shaped function is stable until relatively high capacities, those at which the optimal function becomes linear. In a negatively skewed environment, increasing capacity shifts 𝑢 * from an Sshaped curve to a convex form before ultimately converging to a linear function. This highlights the fact that for reasonably large ranges of possible rewards, very low-capacity choosers universally show the Sshaped utility function as optimal. As capacity increases above this very low level, we see the expected pattern of risk-aversion-like curvature in right-skewed environments and the expected pattern of riskseeking-like curvature in left-skewed environments. Figure 11 plots these same analyses, but here for a chooser minimizing their expected error rate. These functions remain largely similar, but it should be noted that they transition slightly more rapidly to the linear shape than in the reward maximization setting.

These variations suggest that while increased capacity aligns decision-making strategies across both frameworks, constraints on capacity drive distinct adaptations in the encoding of value.

3.4 Result IV: Maximizing Rewards vs Minimizing Errors

The results from sections 3.2 and 3.3 make it clear that, for the three environments we have examined, it is very difficult to use the shape of the utility function to infer whether the decision-maker is optimizing for average reward or minimizing error. There would be great value in identifying an environment in which the two objective functions are distinct. Woodford and colleagues (Polanía et al., 2019; Woodford, 2014) have conducted experiments that suggest human decision-makers may be seeking to minimize errors. To enhance the strength of those conclusions, it might be of value to identify an environment in which these two objective functions are more distinct. Here, we show that bimodally distributed environments have this property.

Figure 12 plots, using the conventions from Figures 10 and 11, the optimal utility functions for the bimodal environment shown in panel A. Note that while the functions shown in B and C have similar shapes, the absolute magnitudes of the utility functions are quite different in the central region. This is especially clear if we examine the low-capacity choosers. While in no way does this imply that the environment in panel A is optimal for making this discrimination, it does suggest that our approach offers a tool for selecting an environment for testing the objectives of choosers.

Figure 12: The optimal utility functions for a bimodally distributed environment. Follows conventions in Figures 8 and 9.

Panel A shows a bimodally distributed environment where rewards of value 2 and 6 are both highly valued. Panel B shows the reward-maximizing utility functions. Note that the function is flat in the center where rewards are rare. Panel C plots the functions for error minimization. Note that the absolute levels of the utility functions for the two different objectives vary significantly, particularly at low capacities.

Figure 13 summarizes this conclusion by directly comparing optimal utility functions for 4 different environments, the 3 canonical environments, and our bimodal environment. We plot here the optimal functions for a 2𝑆𝐷 chooser. These highlight the clear advantages of selecting an appropriate environment for this kind of test.

3.5 Result V: As Choice Set Size Increases, Optimal Utility Functions Steepen and Shift to the Right

A limit of the analytic approach employed up to this point is that it cannot identify optimal utility functions when there are more than two alternatives in the choice set. Here, we show that a strategy of exhaustive simulation, which does not have this limitation, can be used to identify optimal utility functions under essentially any conditions (details in the Methods section). We first validated our Monte Carlo solution by confirming that it replicates the results of the analytic method for binary choice problems across all three canonical environments; this validation is presented in Supplementary Materials Section B. Having established the accuracy of our solution we next investigate the effect of increasing choice-set size on the shape of the optimal utility function.

Figure 14 shows how capacity and choice set size interact in three different environments. The first row of optimal utility functions replicates our earlier findings. For a choice between two options, optimal utility functions show diminishing curvature as capacity increases. The third row of the figure shows how these optimal utility functions change when four options are drawn at random from the choice environment and the decision-maker must select a single option from this four-option set. The fourth and fifth rows present functions for choice set sizes of 6 and 10. Notice that as the choice set size grows, the functions noticeably steepen to the right. This is a key insight that has not yet been the subject of much inquiry by economists or psychologists. The goal of the utility function that maximizes the average rate of return is to discriminate effectively amongst the highest valued of the available options. As the number of options in the choice set grows, the likelihood that at least one option will be very highly valued also grows. This puts a premium on making an effective discrimination amongst the most highly valued options, causing the functions to steepen to the right as the size of the choice set grows. The novel implication of this finding is that for an optimal chooser, risk attitudes should depend on choice set size.

4. Empirical Evaluation

>Empirical Evaluation

4.1 Dataset

To provide an initial empirical assessment of our framework and to define the procedures required for fitting empirical data to our theory, we reanalyzed data from a previously collected two-stage experiment (Kurtz-David et al., 2024). That experiment was designed to examine how value representations adapt when the statistical structure of the choice environment is changed, a core feature of our theory. In Stage 1 of that existing experiment, a stage used to preselect homogeneous and reliable choosers, participants reported their willingness to pay for each of 33 50-50 lotteries using a Becker-DeGroot-Marschak (BDM) method, with one randomly selected trial implemented for payment. These valuations were used to estimate an individual subjective-value function using a power-utility specification. For subjects proceeding to Stage 2, participants were selected whose risk aversion during the BDM bidding procedure (which is known to be distinct from their risk aversion level during choice) was narrowly bounded (𝑝𝑜𝑤𝑒𝑟 𝑢𝑡𝑖𝑙𝑖𝑡𝑦 𝑐𝑢𝑟𝑣𝑎𝑡𝑢𝑟𝑒 𝑎𝑡 0.9 < 𝜌 < 1.1). In Stage 2, on two separate days, subjects made binary choices between 50-50 binary lotteries with two different monetary outcomes each of which ranged from $0 to $60, with 320 decision problems presented on each day. Only the distribution of lottery values differed across the days: values were drawn either from a Uniform distribution or from a Pareto Type III distribution, with the order of the two environments counterbalanced across participants. Because each participant experienced both environments, the dataset allows us to examine how estimates of representational capacity (and the shape of the optimal utility function) change within the same individual as the environmental statistics change. This permits us to examine two properties of the capacity estimates obtained from our framework: 1) whether individual differences in estimated capacity are preserved across environments, consistent with capacity reflecting a relatively stable individual constraint on reward representation; and 2) whether the level of estimated capacity also changes with the statistical structure of the environment, potentially reflecting differences in the benefits of allocating cognitive resources.

4.2 Analysis

4.2.1 Constructing the Individual Error-matrices

Recall that our theory was specifically designed to predict precisely when and how errors (failures to pick the higher valued option) occur, this differs from most standard models. We also treat the objective value axis as discrete in our theory, another important difference. For each participant, we therefore first discretized the range of lottery expected values into subject-specific value bins. To ensure that the two environments were evaluated on a common value scale, the bin boundaries were defined as evenly spaced quantiles of choice problems using the participant's lottery values in the Uniform environment and then held fixed for the Pareto environment. The expected values of both options from all Uniform trials were thus pooled and divided into 12 equally populated bins using a simple quantile-based binning procedure with the lower and upper boundaries fixed at the minimum ($0) and maximum ($60) values encountered. These same 12 bins were then also employed in the Pareto environment. The midpoint of each bin was used as its representative value.

For each environment, every binary-choice trial was thus assigned to a pair of value bins according to the expected values of its two options 7 . A choice was classified as an error if the participant selected the option with the lower expected value. For every choice-pair (or more precisely for every choice-pair bin), we calculated both the number of observed choices involving that pair and the proportion of those choices that were errors. This yielded a symmetric empirical error matrix for each participant for each environment. The trials in which both options fell within the same value bin, the diagonal cells, were excluded from model fitting as errors are not possible in those bins. To avoid fitting to error rates determined by a single observation, cells containing fewer than two trials were also excluded from our analysis. Only one triangular half of the symmetric matrix is presented, which captures all possible pairwise choices. An example of such a matrix for a subject can be seen in Figure 16D.

4.2.2 Computing Expected Error Rates as a Function of Capacity

Recall that our theory rests on the notion that choosers adapt their utility functions to the current environment in order to maximize overall returns. In order to most precisely specify the environment each chooser encountered, we used how often each value bin appeared in the participant's choices to describe the specific value environment that chooser experienced. For each bin (and hence choice problem), we counted how often an error was observed in that bin and how many total problems were encountered by that chooser in that bin. Dividing errors by the total number of encountered problems we derived an error rate and a total count for each bin. This gave us the probability of encountering each value bin in that environment and the error rate observed in that bin for that chooser.

Our goal is to derive, for the observed choice environment defined by the encounter rates, optimal utility functions for every possible capacity level. Once these optimal utility functions have been derived for this specific environment at each possible capacity level, we can convert these optimal utility functions into predicted error rates that should have been observed in each bin if an ideal chooser was employing that optimal utility function, and hence the capacity level associated with that utility function. Using the binomial likelihood to correct for the number of encounters, we can then ask which theoretical error matrix (each associated with a different capacity) best matches the observed error rates produced by a given subject.

Following our theory we thus computed a monotonic utility function that maximized expected earnings at each capacity level, calculated independently for each environment encountered by each chooser over a grid of capacities from 1 to 20 in steps of 0.5. Figure 16A shows all these optimal utility functions for one example subject. A capacity of 0 here corresponds to a random chooser. A few examples of this optimal utility function at selected capacities (𝐶 = 20, 7, 4, 2.5) are shown in Figure 16B. The resulting distances between represented values in the optimal utility function were used to determine the probability of making an error in each value bin. Thus, independently for every subject, a predicted (theoretical) error matrix was generated for each level of capacity, examples of which can be seen in Figure 16C. Here, each error matrix corresponds to the optimal utility function in Panel B for the respective value of capacity. Next, we compared each of the theoretical error matrices with the participant's actual empirical error matrix which can be seen in Figure 16D. Our goal was to ask which theoretical error matrix was most likely to have led to the observed empirical error matrix, thus specifying a best estimate of the capacity allocated by each individual chooser to a given environment. In a statistical sense our procedure reduces to using the theoretical matrix to specify the weighted coin that the subject should have flipped in each bin, and then using the binomial likelihood to simply ask how likely it is that an observed error matrix derived from any given theoretical matrix -allowing for the number of observations in each bin. Thus, for a cell (𝑖, 𝑗), 𝑛 #, is the number of trials, 𝑘 #, is the number of observed errors, and 𝑝 #, (𝐶) is the predicted probability of error at a capacity of 𝐶. We evaluated the prediction using the binomial log-likelihood, which are summed across all the eligible non-diagonal cells as:

The participant's best-fitting capacity is formally defined as the capacity that maximizes this summed loglikelihood. This procedure is carried out independently for the Uniform and Pareto environments, yielding two capacity estimates for each participant. Figure 16E shows these summed binomial log-likelihoods of the observed error matrix resulting from a given optimal utility function at each capacity value. The capacity with the highest log-likelihood value is then selected as the best-fitting capacity value for that environment (𝐶 = 7 in the example). The examples reveal substantial heterogeneity across subjects in both the frequency and structure of choice errors. The log-likelihoods identify a distinct best-fitting capacity within each environment. For example, the participant in the first row makes comparatively more errors as can be seen in the corresponding error matrices. Their estimated capacity is thus towards the lower end of possible capacities, a capacity of 4 in Uniform and a capacity of 1 in Pareto. Also, note that their performance is very close to a random chooser in the Pareto environment. The participant in the fourth row of Figure 17 is a nearly perfect subject who makes almost no errors in the trials and their best estimated capacity is 17.5 in Uniform and 17 in Pareto environment. As choice errors decrease, the best-fitting capacity generally increases. It is important to note that the estimated capacity differs between the Uniform and Pareto conditions, but the relative ordering of these example subjects is preserved, individuals with lower capacity in one environment tend to have lower capacity in the other, whereas higher capacity individuals remain comparatively high across environments. This relationship is examined formally at the population level in the following section.

4.2.3 Example Subjects and Subject-Level Analysis

4.2.4 Population-Level Analysis

At the population level, we first examined whether our model identifies stable individual differences in representational capacity. If capacity reflects an underlying constraint on reward representation, choosers with relatively high estimated capacity in one environment should also have relatively high capacity in another, despite differences in the statistical structure of the choice environment. We therefore examined whether the capacity estimates obtained independently in the Uniform and Pareto environments were correlated across participants. The estimated capacitiesfoot_4 in the Uniform and Pareto environments were, as predicted, correlated across participants with a Pearson correlation coefficient of 0.792 (𝑝 = 0.0003) (Figure 18A). Participants with high estimated capacity (or equivalently, a lower cost per unit of allocated capacity) in one environment also had high capacity in the other. This suggests that the capacity parameter captures relatively stable individual differences in decision-making precision despite changes in the reward environment. Interestingly, although relative capacity rankings were largely preserved, participants generally had lower estimated capacities in the Pareto environment than in the Uniform environment. The regression equation 𝐶 ? @ABC* = 0.57𝐶 -D#E*A" + 0.37, captures this pattern: participants with higher capacity in Uniform also had higher capacity in Pareto, but the estimated levels were generally lower.

We next examined the earnings associated with the estimated representations (Figure 18B). In both environments, participants' actual earnings were close to the maximum earnings predicted by our framework at their estimated capacity. Relative to the optimal earnings in the Uniform environment, optimal earnings in the Pareto environment were 21.3% lower, while participants' actual earnings were 24.9% lower. Therefore, the environment associated with lower estimated capacities also offered lower potential earnings. One possible explanation is that participants adjust cognitive resources allocated to a choice problem according to the benefits of additional precision. If greater capacity is costly, lower potential returns could reduce the incentive to allocate additional capacity. Although the present analysis does not directly identify the costs of capacity, the observed pattern is consistent with this interpretation. A formal model of endogenous capacity allocation is developed in Glimcher et al. (2026).

We note that we have also examined a standard expected-utility model using these same data for comparison. The full model specification, cross-environment parameter analysis, and comparison of the EU curvature (𝛼) and noise (𝛿) parameters with the capacity estimates from our framework are provided in Section C of the Supplementary Materials. In that section we address the challenges of directly comparing our Bernoulli-error analysis and a traditional fitted parameter model. In general, we find that our model performs comparably to EU on this particular dataset.

5. Discussion

Biologists and engineers think of decision-making as a mechanism directed towards achieving an objective goal. These approaches descend from Pascal, who defined a decision-maker's objective goal as maximizing how much good-stuff they have in the long-run (Pascal, 1670). The notion that human decisions are guided by purely subjective goals, captured by an idiosyncratic utility function that does not maximize how much stuff you have at the end of the day, entered choice theory in the 1700s. In developing that approach, Bernoulli (Bernoulli, 1738) was motivated by the observation that humans showed an aversion to risks in the famous St. Petersburg game. Bernoulli interpreted this behavior as inconsistent with the goal of maximizing objective average rates of return. In the years that followed, subjective utility functions became the standard for psychologists as well as for economists. By the late 1900s, with the work of Kahneman and Tversky (Kahneman & Tversky, 1979; Tversky & Kahneman, 1981) and their development of an (intransitive) value function, the notion that human decision-making was subjective, could not be considered optimizing, and could not be construed as driven by any clear objective function had become widely accepted.

There were, however, elements of this approach that raised persistent challenging questions. Matthew Rabin (Rabin, 2000), for example, showed that if one uses the curvature of the human utility function measured in the laboratory to predict human behavior when making very large purchases of durable goods, it predicts a level of risk aversion that is never observed. What the Rabin Paradox revealed is that the risk aversion implied by the standard utility function approach derived in the laboratory and those derived from realworld analysis of major purchases are incompatible.

Here, we argue that this comes from a misunderstanding of just why the human utility function arises in nature. In our work (Glimcher et al., 2026) and other recent work like it (Barretto-García et al., 2023; Oprea, 2024), it is hypothesized that the curvature of the human utility function for small stakes decisions has nothing to do with a desire to avoid risk. For a decision maker with limited cognitive capacity, a curved utility function (which produces what can be interpreted as an aversion to risk) is required if one's goal is to maximize how much good-stuff one has on average. This leads us to suggest that, at least for small stakes, the utility function is not a goal, but rather a tool. It is not an objective in and of itself, but a reward encoding strategy used by the nervous system to achieve a different and well-specified objective function. We believe that this is our key contribution, and an extension of earlier work that has explored similar themes (Barretto-García et al., 2023; Frydman & Jin, 2021; Glimcher, 2011; Khaw et al., 2021; Netzer, 2009; Netzer et al., 2025; Polanía et al., 2019; Rayo & Becker, 2007; Robson, 2001; Robson et al., 2023; Woodford, 2014). A separation of the objective and utility functions, and a reinterpretation of the utility function as being an empirical tool dynamically configured by the human (and animal) decisional architecture in service of the objective function -at least for small stakes day-to-day decision-making -is, we believe, a necessary and fundamental reanalysis of the utility function that has been gaining traction in the last fifteen years. In addition to this primary contribution, we can also draw what we believe to be six significant conclusions about the shape of the optimal utility function.

5.1 Summary of Major Findings

5.1.1 Reward Distributions Determine Optimal Utility

The first of our observations is that the distribution of possible rewards, the context of the choice, determines the shape of the optimal utility function for choosers with limited cognitive capacity. For choosers facing a world in which small rewards are prevalent and larger rewards are rare (right-skewed distributions), optimal utility functions are concave and resemble the kinds of risk-averse utility functions Bernoulli favored. In fact, if we write out the specific distribution of possible rewards in the famous St Petersburg gamefoot_5 , we discover that the optimal utility function is almost exactly the function Bernoulli proposed (𝑙𝑜𝑔 (𝑥)). Bernoulli's utility function maximizes Pascal's objective for a noisy chooser facing a St Petersburg game-like distribution of possible outcomes.

In contrast, when choosers face a uniformly distributed set of rewards, the optimal utility function is sigmoidal. The sigmoidal utility function was first widely popularized by Kahneman and Tversky (Kahneman & Tversky, 1979), but see also Savage and Friedman (Friedman & Savage, 1948) who argued that Bernoulli's function could not account for the behavior of their subjects. One cannot help but note that Kahneman and Tversky performed most of their experiments with environments in which rewards were distributed uniformly. Environments in which rewards are uniformly distributed, even in the absence of true risk, create a new shape for the utility function that mirrors the one Kahneman and Tversky encountered.

Finally, we found that if choosers face a left-skewed distribution, the optimal utility function is in fact convex. Choosers in these environments should show a utility structure classically associated with riskseeking behavior. In traditional economics, this kind of risk-seeking behavior is often referred to as a violation of second-order stochastic dominance. What this finding suggests is that violations of secondorder stochastic dominance in a left-skewed environment, long treated as irrational, may be much more reasonable than has been generally supposed.

The environments considered here are intentionally simplified. A natural question is how this environmental sensitivity operates in the real world, where decisions from many different contexts are randomly interleaved and choosers face the hard problem of selecting an estimate of the environment in which they are operating. While our framework does not include a specific description of how this selection is made, we infer from existing work on this problem that adaptation to the environment is best conceptualized as a slow, implicit process, likely analogous to gain control in sensory systems (Carandini & Heeger, 2012). In such a specification the utility function reflects a gradually updated approximation to the aggregate reward distribution experienced over the relevant timescale. This interpretation is consistent with empirical work showing that value representations shift in response to recently encountered reward statistics through mechanisms of range adaptation and divisive normalization (Barretto-García et al., 2023; Khaw et al., 2021; Polanía et al., 2019; Webb, Glimcher & Louie, 2021). How precisely the brain performs this implicit averaging, and over what timescales, remains an important direction for future empirical work and likely is a source of significant inter-individual variation in the selected utility function expressed by different choosers.

5.1.2 Capacity Determines Both Utility and Earnings

Our second class of findings relates to the relationship between cognitive capacity, operationalized as the magnitude of the internal noise in the brain's representation of reward magnitude, and 1) the shape of the utility function and 2) the impact of noise on earnings. We find that as cognitive capacity increases (or equivalently as internal noise decreases), utility functions in all three straighten. This is an almost trivial observation. Pascal demonstrated four centuries ago that a straight utility function was return maximizing for any environment in a chooser with infinite capacity. This is what we observe. As noise goes to zero, optimal utility functions shift towards the straight lines Pascal defined as optimal for his noiseless choosers. What is not trivial is that the nonlinear utility functions that emerge at low to moderate capacity levels are not imperfect approximations to the straight-line ideal but genuinely optimal strategies in their own right.

Much more interesting than this is to examine how reductions in noise change the actual earnings of subjects. Many hold the intuition that if choosers are very noisy, then they behave randomly and earn very little. Our findings run against this intuition. Increases in capacity from 2 to 3, and perhaps even to 4 standard deviations do improve earnings, but much more slowly than one might expect -as long as the chooser is allowed to adapt their utility function to their specific capacity level. Even more interesting is the observation that above about 4 standard deviations, increases in capacity have very small impacts on overall earnings. This has, we believe, huge implications for biological choosers. If one is creating an internal representation of value with a finite biological system that effectively employs just 2 standard deviations in a left-skewed environment, one outperforms a random chooser by 7%. Doubling the cognitive capacity (roughly doubling the biological cost of the encoding system (Glimcher, 2022)) yields only a 2% additional increment in earnings. What has often been treated as a limitation of biological decision-making systems may instead reflect a rational equilibrium, in which the brain operates at the minimum precision level needed to achieve near-optimal earnings, reserving metabolic resources for other demands. In Glimcher et al. (2026) we formalize this insight, arguing that choosers or evolution may in fact select a precision level that exactly balances cognitive costs against the benefits of higher precision to maximize their net return optimally.

These results also raise the question of the extent to which human decision makers might intentionally reduce their cognitive costs, reduce their cognitive capacity when in low-stakes environments. If we think of cognitive costs as being roughly fixed and monotonic, we can assess the degree to which capacity is adjustable by simply repeating the same experiment at different payoff levels. As we show in some detail in (Glimcher et al., 2026), such experiments could even allow us to determine the cost of capacity and the exact structure of our hidden cognitive cost function. Using this approach in the companion paper, we show how an optimal chooser facing a fixed noise cost can select both a capacity and a utility function optimally. This approach allows us, essentially, to eliminate all free parameters from our model and to treat the selection of an optimal utility function as a fully closed problem.

5.1.3 Maximizing Rewards vs Minimizing Errors

Recently, significant effort has been devoted to assessing whether human choice behavior can be better thought of as aimed at minimizing errors or maximizing rewards. Woodford and colleagues (Polanía et al., 2019; Woodford, 2014), amongst others, have tentatively concluded that the two objectives yield such similar optimal choice strategies that it is difficult to empirically resolve this issue.

Our data confirm these conclusions in many, but not all, environments. In uniformly distributed environments, for example, optimal utility functions for maximizing gain and for minimizing errors are almost identical, which might explain why existing experiments have struggled to discriminate between these two objectives. However, they can be discriminated in bimodally distributed environments, particularly at low capacity levels. Our data suggest that an appropriately designed environment can be used to experimentally discriminate between these two objectives.

5.1.4 Generalization to Bigger Environments: Steeper Sigmoids

The bulk of the data we present was computed for environments in which there are only 4 possible prizes that lie equally spaced on the objective value axis. Our fourth general result was developed by examining equally spaced sets of rewards containing more than 4 elements. While there is no conceptual barrier to selecting sets of any size (or employing any spacing on the value axis), larger sets take more computational time. For this reason, we limited this presentation to a maximum of 6 possible evenly spaced rewards (See Glimcher et al., 2026, for 7 possible rewards). As the size of the set of possible rewards grows, the utility functions we encounter become smoother and more classical-looking. For uniformly distributed rewards, we found that the sigmoidal functions also become steeper and generally look more like the classical value function of Kahneman and Tversky. Perhaps surprisingly, we found that even left-skewed distributions can yield sigmoidal optimal utility functions, at very low capacities, suggesting that the sigmoid might not be diagnostic of a uniform environment but rather emerges as a universal feature of low-capacity choosers facing sufficiently rich reward sets.

5.1.5 Larger Choice Sets Shift Optimal Utility Functions to the Right

The final result we highlight concerns a variable that has received surprisingly little attention in the utility function literature: the size of the choice set itself. We found that the optimal utility functions steepen and shift to the right as the size of the choice set grows. This makes intuitive sense. As the number of possible draws from the environment increases, the likelihood of encountering at least one option that lies far to the right increases, and the utility function thus shifts to the right to improve accuracy in detecting this best option. This sensitivity of the optimal utility function to choice set size has not, to our knowledge, been previously presented. (Although many studies have examined choice set size (Iyengar & Lepper, 2000; Schwartz, 2004; Webb et al., 2021).)

It should also be noted that these Monte-Carlo-based estimates are not quite as well-behaved as our analytical results. One will notice immediately that estimates of utility function curvature around reward values that are very rarely encountered in the environment can be somewhat noisy. This can be seen both in the color plots of all possible utility functions and in the 'best utility function' plots. This imprecision arises because the Monte-Carlo approach which yields poor estimates of events which are very infrequent. This can be overcome, of course, by using a much larger number of iterations in the simulations.

5.1.6 Empirical Evaluation

Our final general result comes from applying our new framework to an existing dataset in which the same individuals made repeated choices in Uniform and Pareto reward environments. Unlike standard models in which a utility (or value) function and a noise term are fit by some form of a least squares procedure, to test our model we examine the error matrices produced by our subjects directly and compare them to the error matrices predicted by our theory. Testing our theory thus resolves empirically to employing a single free parameter and a binomial theorem-based likelihood analysis to assess goodness of fit. We fit capacity to a subject's observed choice behavior in a three-step process. First, we explicitly define as an error any choice in which the chooser selects the lower valued option. Next, we aggregate the pattern of observed errors into an error matrix. Finally, we compare the empirically observed error matrix to the set of theoretically predicted error matrices which differ in the capacity allocated by the chooser to the choice problem. We perform this comparison using a simple binomial likelihood procedure. The result is a best-fit capacity parameter and an overall likelihood score.

The empirical analysis provides two insights into the role of representational capacity in human choice. First, estimated capacities were strongly correlated across the Uniform and Pareto environments, suggesting that the capacity parameter captures relatively stable individual differences in decision-making precision.

Participants with relatively high capacity in one environment tended to have relatively high capacity in the other. Second, despite this stability in relative capacity, the estimated levels differed across environments, with participants generally exhibiting lower capacity in the Pareto environment. Interestingly, this environment also offered lower potential earnings. One possible interpretation is that choosers adjust the capacity allocated to decision-making in response to the benefits of greater precision, a possibility developed formally in Glimcher et al. (2026). The current results are consistent with this interpretation but do not establish the mechanism underlying capacity allocation.

It is worth noting that models like EU and prospect theory struggle to fit highly stochastic subjects. For these subjects the utility or value function cannot be well defined because the models rely on their noise terms to account for these choices of these choosers rather than relying on the utility function -thus leading to unspecified utility functions for these choosers. In our theory, these low-capacity choosers are a key feature of the model. They are easily and precisely accounted for by our approach. In contrast, our model struggles to define the precise capacity level of choosers who are nearly perfect expected value maximizers. This is because these choosers have, in our model, very high-capacity levels. Whether a chooser has a capacity of 20 or 25 can be hard to distinguish for our model. Said another way, for these choosers of very high capacity the underlying utility functions are all virtually identical making model fitting difficult. In contrast, models like expected utility theory and prospect theory can take advantage of this homogeneity because it is the utility function, rather than the capacity, that they are trying to fit.

Finally, we note that all of these differences can make the two classes of models, standard utility models and our capacity model, hard to compare empirically. The very different fitting procedures, the fact that they can account for different kinds of choosers in different ways, and the different numbers of parameters, all make head-to-head comparisons difficult. One future direction for our research program will be to develop experiments specifically designed to stress test these models against one another.

5.2 Implications for What are Traditionally Considered Risky-Choice Behaviors

The utility analysis presented here has been focused on riskless choice, choices between two certain options. All theoretical derivations and simulations apply exclusively to this domain. While many of the utility curves we recover bear striking similarities in shape to those employed by Bernoulli, the Utilitarians of the 19th Century, and Kahneman and Tversky, nearly all of that research was focused on risky-choice and rested on the assumption that the curvature of the utility functions they observed was specifically about a response to risk. Our finding of essentially identical curvature for the utility function in the absence of risk raises the question of whether a riskless framework can explain phenomena that have traditionally been characterized as specifically related to the domain of risk, a suggestion which builds on recent work by Barretto-García et al. (2023) and Oprea (2024), amongst others.

5.2.1 The Reflection Effect

The reflection effect is, at its core, a claim about the shape of the utility function around a central reference value. In 1981, Kahneman and Tversky (Tversky & Kahneman, 1981) described what they referred to as the Reflection Effect, the observation that gambles of equal magnitude above and below the reference point show roughly equal and opposite risk preferences. More broadly, this is often taken to imply that for a given chooser, risk attitudes are symmetric but inverted about the reference point. If the risk attitude above the reference point is modeled as 𝑢(𝑥) = (𝑥 -𝑟𝑝) F , the risk preferences of the same subject can be modeled below the reference point as 𝑢(𝑥) = -(𝑥 -𝑟𝑝) 1F.

While Kahneman and Tversky made this characterization using risky lotteries as the objects of choice, it is of some note that our framework recovers this structure precisely as optimal under specific conditions without any appeal to risk. As Figure 10F shows, a perfectly symmetrical function can be optimal for a perfectly uniform environment with the inflection point of that sigmoid naturally defining the reference point, but non-uniform environments can require sigmoids that are non-symmetrical. In our framework, optimality depends critically on both the capacity of the chooser and the distributional structure of the environment and can yield curved cardinal utility functions derived from the patterns of errors a chooser makes, rather than from indifference points amongst the risky lotteries employed by Kahneman and Tversky.

Given this, it seems relevant to note that the actual patterns of observed utility function curvature are highly variable from subject to subject and environment to environment (Bucher & Brandenburger, 2022; Glimcher & Tymula, 2023). In Chung et al. (2019), we systematically examined utility function curvature in the gain and loss domains and found very little evidence for a reliable reflection of risk attitudes at the single-subject level. Only at the population level did we see clear symmetry. This observed heterogeneity has often led to challenges to the reflection effect. Under our assumptions, optimality depends on the specific environment encountered by the decision-maker, the decision-maker's beliefs about that environment, and the capacity of the decision-maker.

5.2.2 Loss Aversion (Gain-Loss Asymmetry)

Another fundamental element of behavioral decision science is Loss Aversion (Kahneman et al., 1991; Kahneman & Tversky, 1979), also known as a Gain-Loss Asymmetry (Plott & Zeiler, 2007). Where the reflection effect concerns symmetric curvature, loss aversion concerns asymmetric curvature. In 1979, Kahneman and Tversky noted that human decision-makers were not indifferent between a sure gain of $0 and a lottery which had equal likelihoods of yielding a gain of $10 and a loss of $10. This was puzzling. If the human utility function is symmetrical about $0, the equal losses and gains should cancel each other out and choosers should be indifferent between these two options. Instead, humans show an asymmetry in the assessment of gains and losses under a wide range of conditions. To understand this phenomena, early prospect theorists made two strong assumptions: First, that the reference point (although unmeasured) was fixed in this experiment at $0. Second, that the first derivative of the value function above and below the reference point had an identical absolute value (an assumption known as the reflection effect). Given those two assumptions, the only way to account for these observed phenomena was to hypothesize that "losses loom larger than gains" independent of the curvature of the gain and loss utility functions. Very important to this analysis, however, are these two assumptions: that the reference point is fixed at a fully-known location and that the utility function has fixed and identical degrees of curvature above and below this reference point.

This immediately raises an important caveat when considering empirical tests of loss aversion. These tests almost all rely on assumptions about the exact location of the reference point held by the chooser. To understand this, consider the utility function presented in Figure 10F for an environment with uniformly distributed rewards. By most definitions, the reference point for this function lies midway between 3 and 4. If an experimentalist were to define 4 as the expected reference point when subjects were using this value function, they would observe a gain-loss asymmetry, a kind of loss aversion: If subjects were given a choice between $4 for sure or a 50/50 chance of either $3 or $5, they would prefer the $4 for sure. The asymmetry arises because the value function rises more slowly above 4 than it falls below 4. Were one to repeat the experiment around $3.5, however, the human choice behavior would be perfectly symmetrical and there would be no evidence of loss aversion. This highlights the importance of an experimentalist's definition of the reference point.

Our data does, however, support the notion that the value function can, under some conditions, be quite asymmetric even in the absence of risky lotteries. To see this, compare Figures 13F and 13G. While 13F shows a symmetrical function driven by a uniformly distributed environment, 13G shows a highly asymmetrical function driven by a left-skewed environment. In this construction, however, the loss-gain asymmetry is in no way irrational or puzzling, it is simply a strategy for dealing efficiently with some classes of input distributions and emerges as a feature of decision-makers in the absence of risky lotteries.

Both of these observations suggest that what we call loss aversion can emerge from either a misspecification (by the experimenter) of the reference point, or from an asymmetrical value function driven by the chooser's efficient behavior in a non-uniform environment. More importantly, perhaps, our approach reveals that loss aversion-like behavior can be observed in the absence of lotteries.

5.3 Extensions of Our Framework to Decision Under Risk -Implications for Future Work

Next, we turn to important extensions to our framework into the domain of truly risky choice. It is important to note that what follows are speculative extensions of our findings that are not formally derived within the current framework but which we consider to be highly relevant to this work.

While we do adopt a representation of the environment as probabilistic in this paper, it is important to be aware that we do not here include the notion that the object of an actual choice can be, in essence, a lottery ticket. Extrapolating our approach to prospects that are themselves risky or uncertain requires two additional steps that we have not taken here. First, we must incorporate the notion of a representation of probability (not just utility) inside the chooser, which is itself cognitively costly and capacity-limited. If we extend our approach to include the subjective representation of probabilities, we must ask the question: What is the optimal probability weighting function while at the same time asking: what is the optimal utility function? In a forthcoming presentation we extend our approach to probability weighting functions in this manner.

To address risk in its traditional sense we need to define how choosers should (in a normative sense) represent the environment when it includes probabilistic outcomes. The critical idea here is that for choosers with limited capacity facing lotteries, there are really two kinds of probability: The probability of encountering a lottery (the environment) and the probability of winning a lottery (the outcome probability).

These two probabilities have different impacts on choice and must be handled separately, which may not be immediately obvious.

One is tempted to bundle these two kinds of probability together: To assume that choosers encode a lottery ticket with a 50% chance of winning $10 as an environment that independently includes both a possible reward of $0 with a probability of 50% and possible reward of $10 with a probability of 50%. The drawback of such a simple representation is that it entirely neglects the non-independence of these two outcomesthe fact that one cannot choose either the $0 outcome or the $10 outcome but rather that one must choose them together. To capture the complex non-independence of lottery-like objects one must employ a richer representation of the environment which independently represents these two kinds of probabilities: The probability of encountering a lottery in the environment and the probability of winning that lottery if one selects it.

To study this class of problem using our approach requires an enriched definition of the environment we present in the Methods section. This enriched definition must capture both kinds of probabilities and any arbitrary covariant structure between offers and lotteries.

Mellers' and Tetlock's classic work (Mellers et al., 2015) on this very problem which examined how different individuals show different degrees of consistency and accuracy in how they use probabilities is a key insight for understanding capacity limits in probability representation. Their work reveals that different individuals possess different cognitive capacities for representing probability. This is a finding very closely aligned with our normative observation that individuals would be expected to employ different cognitive capacities for representing subjective value, or utility. Our ongoing work in the domain of probability representation rests heavily on these insights.

Both Vieider and colleagues and Maloney and colleagues have completed beautiful work which is also central to the extension of our approach to the domain of risky lotteries (Vieider, 2024; Zhang et al., 2020).

Their work examines how decisional accuracy depends on the probabilistic structure of the environment. This mirrors much of the work we present here, but with a focus more directly on probabilistic representation. They have devoted significant effort to exploring how distortions of probability might arise as the environmental probability structure is manipulated. This work also serves as a deep foundation for understanding the optimal representation of probability.

5.3.1 The Four-Fold Pattern of Risk Attitudes

One other key feature of human risk attitudes captured by prospect theory is the so-called four-fold pattern. Risk attitudes over lotteries depend not just on whether the prospect lies within the gain or loss domain (relative to the reference point) but also depend on the probability of the outcomes under consideration.

Classically, this is presented as four classes of risk attitudes: 1) Risk aversion for high probability gains, 2) Risk seeking for high probability losses, but also 3) Risk seeking for very low probability gains, and 4) Risk aversion for very low probability losses.

The probability weighting function accounts for this phenomenon by overweighting low probability events and underweighting high probability events. If the four-fold pattern is indeed a robust feature of human choice behavior (a point which is in debate), it is important to note that prospect theory requires the probability weighting function to achieve this pattern specifically because the value function is considered stationary. In prospect theory, the value function cannot change shape in response to changes in the choice environment and in most experiments, the value of the reference point is treated as fixed for the duration of the experiment.

In the approach we present here, both of these restrictions on the value function have been relaxed. The shape of the utility function is dependent on both the environment and on cognitive capacity. The numerical value of the reference point, defined as an inflection in the utility function, also depends on the environment. While it is not clear from the work we present here whether the four-fold pattern can emerge from these changes, there is some reason to suspect that it might. When we have previously examined divisive normalization-based models as alternatives to prospect theory (Glimcher & Tymula, 2023), we have found some indication that relaxing these restrictions on the value function may allow a choice system to account for the four-fold pattern without relying on a specific s-shaped distortion of the underlying representation of probability.

5.4 Summary

Traditional theories of decision-making assume that humans possess a fixed utility function that maps objective rewards to subjective value. From Pascal's expected value to Bernoulli's expected utility theory, they sought to describe how rational agents ought to behave but struggled to reconcile the inconsistencies observed in real human choices. Modern predictive models such as prospect theory improved the descriptive power of choice theory but largely abandoned normative explanation, leaving unanswered the question of why these irrationalities occur. In this paper, we propose a normative framework that reconciles these apparent inconsistencies by suggesting that the utility function itself is an adaptive, rational construct shaped by a number of underlying constraints, including environmental statistics and representational precision.

Our framework proposes that the decision-maker, faced with finite representational precision, optimally selects a task-appropriate utility function to maximize long-run average earnings or minimize decision errors for the current environment. Through analytical derivations and Monte Carlo simulations, we show that the classical utility functions with which all scholars are familiar emerge naturally as optimal encoding strategies under varying environmental and capacity constraints. Concave utilities optimize performance in environments dominated by frequent small rewards; sigmoidal utilities in uniformly distributed contexts; and convex utilities in environments where large rewards are most common. As precision increases, these functions converge toward linearity, reflecting a diminishing need for a nonlinear transformation of value in order to optimize the underlying representation.

Further, we quantify the incremental gains from expanding cognitive capacity and find them to be modest once the utility function is optimally adjusted to available capacity. This finding suggests that bounded rationality may instead reflect a rational equilibrium between computational cost and behavioral efficiency. The brain, in essence, might well employ the minimal precision necessary to achieve near-optimal earnings given its energetic and informational constraints.

Our findings suggest that when utility is treated as a flexible encoding tool rather than a fixed psychological quantity, bounded rationality becomes not a limitation but an efficient design principle. The diversity of observed risk attitudes and utility functions across individuals and species can be seen as reflecting an optimal adaptation. By reframing the utility function as an endogenous, rationally selected encoding mechanism, our framework offers a bridge between prescriptive and descriptive theories of choice.
