The participant in the fourth row of Figure17is a nearly perfect subject who makes almost no errors in the trials and their best estimated capacity is 17.5 in Uniform and 17 in Pareto environment. As choice errors decrease, the best-fitting capacity generally increases. It is important to note that the estimated capacity differs between the Uniform and Pareto conditions, but the relative ordering of these example subjects is preserved, individuals with lower capacity in one environment tend to have lower capacity in the other, whereas higher capacity individuals remain comparatively high across environments. This relationship is examined formally at the population level in the following section.

Figure 17 :

Figure 17: Four representative subjects illustrating individual-level fits in the Uniform and Pareto environments. Panel A: Empirical error matrices for the four subjects in the Uniform environment; color indicates the observed error rate, and numbers indicate the number of trials contributing to each cell. Panel B: Corresponding summed binomial log-likelihood across capacities in the Uniform environment. The green dashed line marks the best-fitting capacity and the red dashed line the random-chooser benchmark. Panel C: Empirical error matrices for the same subjects in the Pareto environment. Panel D: Corresponding summed binomial log-likelihood across capacities in the Pareto environment, with the best-fitting capacity and random-choice benchmark indicated as in Panel B.

Figure 18 :

Figure 18: Population-level capacity estimates and earnings. Panel A: Best-fitting capacity in the Pareto environment plotted against best-fitting capacity in the Uniform environment for each participant. The dashed black line shows the fitted linear relationship (slope = 0.57, intercept = 0.37). Capacity estimates (as rank order across subjects) were strongly correlated across environments with a Pearson correlation coefficient of 0.792 (𝑝 = 0.0003). Panel B: Mean earnings for a perfect chooser who makes no errors and actual observed earnings in the Uniform and Pareto environments; error bars indicate SEM. The right axis expresses earnings as a percentage of the Uniform-optimal benchmark, with arrows indicating the 21.3% and 24.9% reductions for Pareto-optimal and Pareto-actual earnings, respectively.

We abandon the notion that people are intentionally risk averse on purpose for the current paper. This makes our findings most relevant to situations like the small stakes decisions which are typically encountered in laboratory research projects, and less relevant to those major life decisions like picking a car, a house, or a spouse, where risk-aversion may be seen as more normatively rational.

This is the traditional 'more-is-better' rule around which nearly all choice theories are structured, one major exception being the choice theory of Markowitz(Markowitz, 1952). As will be obvious, our approach can be trivially generalized to include nonmonotonic utility functions, although non-monotonic utility functions are almost never optimal tools for maximizing objective outcomes.

We use the term analytic here to distinguish this approach from the Monte Carlo simulation method described in Section 2.3. For any candidate utility function and any pair of rewards, the probability of an error and the expected earnings can be computed exactly as a function of the normal CDF, with no approximation involved. The exhaustive search is then conducted over a discretized space

Recall that our choosers were preselected to show close to expected value maximization during the BDM procedure.

Participants whose best-fitting capacity reached the upper bound of the tested range 𝐶 = 20 in any of the environments, were excluded from the population-level analysis, because their capacity could not be reliably identified beyond this ceiling.

We need to acknowledge that the St. Petersburg game involves a risky lottery, and that our assessment of the optimal environment here involves a risky environment, but not risky lotteries. This is an important distinction and one to which we devote the next section of the discussion.
